pages.body:
Attention is a soft lookup. A query is compared against a set of keys, and each comparison produces a score. Those scores become weights, and the output is a weighted average of the values attached to those keys. Nothing is selected outright; everything is blended in proportion to how well it matched.

It sits first on this page for a structural reason. Every other operation in the Transformer works on one position at a time. Strip attention out and each token runs through its own feed-forward network knowing nothing about any other token — the two stacks in [[fig-1]] would collapse into a pile of independent per-position MLPs. Attention is the only operation in the model that moves information between positions.

### The operation

Start with the shapes. Pack the queries into a matrix $Q$ of shape $n \times d_k$, the keys into $K$ of shape $m \times d_k$, and the values into $V$ of shape $m \times d_v$.

Queries and keys share the dimension $d_k$, and they have to, because the two get dotted together. The counts $n$ and $m$ are independent: $n$ queries asking, $m$ key-value pairs to ask of.

Then $QK^\top$ is an $n \times m$ matrix. One row per query, one column per key. Every query has been scored against every key, in one matrix multiply.

Three steps remain. Divide every entry by $\sqrt{d_k}$. Apply [[softmax]] along each row, which turns that row's $m$ scores into $m$ weights summing to one. Multiply the result by $V$.

The output is $n \times d_v$. Row $i$ is query $i$'s blend of the values: the weights in row $i$ of the softmax, applied to the $m$ rows of $V$.

That whole sequence is a single line of algebra, [[eq-attention]], and [[fig-2]] draws the same line box by box.

Now look at what is *not* in that line. There are no learned parameters anywhere in it. Dot, scale, softmax, multiply — every step is fixed. All of the learning sits upstream, in the linear maps that produce $Q$, $K$ and $V$ ([[attention-projection-matrices]]).

That is why one function can serve three different jobs. [[encoder-self-attention]], [[masked-decoder-self-attention]] and [[encoder-decoder-attention]] are all the same computation. The only thing that changes between them is which tensors arrive as the queries and which arrive as the keys and values ([[queries-keys-values]]).

### The three choices, and their costs

Three decisions are buried in that line: how pairs are scored, why the scores are shrunk, and what the averaging costs. Take them in that order.

First, the scorer. The [[compatibility-function|compatibility function]] is a plain dot product. The standing alternative was [[additive-attention|a small feed-forward net with one hidden layer]], run on the query and key together.

The paper's argument for the dot product is speed, not accuracy. It grants that the two are of comparable theoretical complexity. The difference is that scoring all pairs by dot product is one matrix multiply, and matrix multiplies have heavily optimised kernels behind them. The claim is about wall-clock time, and it is not pushed further than that.

Second, the scale factor. Divide the scores by $\sqrt{d_k}$ and you have the Transformer's attention. Leave the division out and you have ordinary [[dot-product-attention]]. That factor is the only difference between the two.

On why it helps, the paper hedges, and the hedge is worth reading as written. It *suspects* that for large $d_k$ the dot products grow large in magnitude, which pushes the softmax into regions where its gradients are very small. The support offered is a footnote variance argument rather than an experiment ([[sqrt-dk-scaling]]).

Third, the averaging — and this one is a cost, not a benefit. Attention's output is a weighted average, and averaging discards information. Section 2 states it plainly: a constant-length path between positions comes "at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions."

Blend many positions into one vector and the distinctions between them can smear ([[attention-averaging-resolution-cost]]).

[[multi-head-attention]] is the stated counter. Instead of one attention over the full model width, run $h$ of them in parallel, each in its own learned subspace, with $h = 8$.

The widths follow from that. $d_{model}$ is 512 and there are 8 heads, so each head gets $512/8 = 64$ dimensions: $d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h = 64$. Because each head is eight times narrower, the total compute stays roughly constant. Eight separate averages instead of one, at about the same price.

The evidence for these choices is uneven, and the pieces are worth separating.

[[table-3]] row A is the direct support. Head count is varied with total computation held fixed, and single-head attention comes out 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting. Quality also falls off when heads get too numerous, so there is a middle rather than a monotone gain. All of it on one dev set.

Row B cuts the other way. Shrinking $d_k$ hurts quality, and the authors read that as a hint that the dot product may be too crude a compatibility function. That is an argument against their own first choice, reported rather than resolved.

[[fig-3]] and [[fig-5]] are the thinnest evidence on the page. Each is a single hand-picked sentence with its attention patterns drawn on it. The paper says heads "seem" to track structure — its word, not a stronger one — and it measures nothing ([[attention-interpretability]]).

pages.body:
Beam search is the search procedure that turns the trained decoder into an actual output sentence. The model on its own never produces a sentence. It produces a probability distribution over the next token, one distribution per step, and something has to turn that stream of distributions into a single finished string.

That something is beam search, and it sits inside every result in the paper. Every quality number reported — [[table-2|the BLEU table]], [[table-3|the ablations]], [[table-4|the parsing leaderboard]] — is the score of a beam-search decode. None of them is the score of the model's raw next-token distribution.

### The step, concretely

The decoder is [[auto-regressive-generation|auto-regressive]]. To score token $t$ it needs tokens $1 \dots t-1$ already fixed and fed back in as decoder input. Decoding is therefore a chain: nothing about position $t$ can be computed until a decision has been made about position $t-1$.

Greedy decoding makes that decision in the cheapest possible way. At each step it takes the single highest-probability token and treats it as final. The price is that a token which looks best in isolation at step 3 can commit the sentence to a continuation that is bad at every step after it, and nothing later in the decode can undo the choice.

Beam search delays the commitment by a few positions instead. It does this by refusing to narrow down to one sentence until several more tokens of evidence have arrived.

Keep a set of $k=4$ live hypotheses — four partial sentences, all still in play. At step $t$, run the [[decoder-stack|decoder]] once for each of the four, and take the [[softmax]] over the whole [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] vocabulary, which is 32K–37K tokens. Four hypotheses against a vocabulary that size gives a $4 \times V$ grid of roughly 150,000 candidate continuations, each with its own score.

Score every continuation by the running sum of log-probabilities along its entire path so far, not by the probability of the token just added. Then keep the top 4 across the whole grid — the top 4 out of all 150,000, not the top 4 within each hypothesis. Discard everything else.

That last detail is what lets the search abandon a line of reasoning. If all four survivors happen to be extensions of the same parent, the other three parents die at that step.

A hypothesis that emits the end-of-sequence symbol is not extended further; it is set aside as finished. When the search stops, the best finished hypothesis is the output. The [[inference-length-limit|length cap]] and early termination bound how long this can run.

There is a bias built into scoring by a running sum. Every step adds one more log-probability, and log-probabilities are negative, so the sum only ever shrinks as a hypothesis grows. A 30-token hypothesis carries 30 such terms; a 20-token one carries 20. Compared head to head, the shorter candidate wins partly on being shorter.

Left alone, the search would systematically prefer short outputs. The [[length-penalty|length penalty]] corrects for this by dividing a hypothesis's score by a function of its length, at strength $\alpha = 0.6$ here.

The exact divisor is not written down in this paper. That divisor, and the rest of the decoder around it — including its [[beam-search-pruning-and-termination|pruning and early-termination rules]] and the [[coverage-penalty|coverage penalty]], which the Transformer does not use — are defined in GNMT [38]. That is where [[length-normalization-penalty|the formula]] lives.

### What it costs and what the evidence actually shows

Two separate questions follow: what beam 4 costs at inference time, and what the paper does and does not establish about what it buys. The cost is easy to state.

Beam 4 runs four decoder forward passes per step instead of one, and keeps four sets of cached keys and values instead of one. So it costs roughly $4\times$ the decoder compute and KV memory of greedy decoding.

What the extra width does not buy is any reduction in depth. The four hypotheses are extended alongside each other within a step, but the steps themselves still run one after another: producing an $n$-token output takes $n$ sequential steps no matter the beam size.

That is the asymmetry the paper lives with. Training parallelizes across positions; inference does not.

On the benefit side, the paper says beam size and $\alpha$ were picked on the development set, and it gives no sweep — no BLEU-against-beam-size table, no ablation on $\alpha$. How much either choice buys is therefore not measured here.

One thing can still be said about the comparison itself. Beam 4 is also what the baselines in [[table-2]] used, so the reported gaps are not an artifact of the Transformer decoding differently from its competitors.

The one visible signal about beam size comes from [[table-4]]. Beam size was among the handful of knobs re-tuned for [[constituency-parsing|parsing]], a task whose outputs are long, have to come out bracket-balanced, and are structurally constrained in a way translations are not.

That re-tuning is a hint that the right beam is task-dependent. It is not a demonstration — the paper reports the setting it landed on, not the effect of moving away from it.

For parsing the paper settles on a beam of 21 with $lpha = 0.3$, and raises the output cap to input length + 300. Set beside translation's beam of 4, $lpha = 0.6$ and input length + 50, all three decode settings move the same way: a wider search, a weaker correction against length, and considerably more room to run before the cap bites. That fits an output that is longer and more tightly constrained than a translation.

One further entanglement is worth tracking, though it does not reach every number. The main results are decoded on a [[checkpoint-averaging|checkpoint-averaged]] model rather than on any single trained checkpoint, so the averaging and the search sit together in those scores and nothing in the paper pulls them apart. The model variations are the exception: those rows were decoded with beam search but without averaging, which is what makes them comparable to each other rather than to the headline figures.

BLEU is the number every quality claim in this paper is stated in. The two headline results are BLEU scores: 28.4 on WMT 2014 English-to-German, and 41.8 on English-to-French. Every row of [[table-2]] is a BLEU score, and every delta in [[table-3]] is a difference between two of them.

What it measures is n-gram overlap. It scores a [[machine-translation|translation]] by how much of its n-gram content also turns up in human reference translations. So it grades the tokens the decoder actually emitted, not the probabilities the model assigned to them. That distinction is small to state and does most of the work in the second half of this page.

### The computation

Start with one n-gram size at a time. For each $n$ from 1 to 4, take every n-gram in the candidate output and count how many of them also occur in a reference. Those counts are clipped: an n-gram gets credit at most the number of times it appears in any one reference. Clipping is what stops a degenerate output from farming the count — emitting "the" fifteen times cannot buy fifteen matches when the reference has "the" twice.

Now divide. The clipped match count goes over the total number of n-grams of that size in the candidate, and the ratio is the modified precision $p_n$. There are four of these, one per n-gram size.

The order of operations matters here. Clipped counts and candidate totals are summed across the whole test corpus first, and only then divided. BLEU is a corpus statistic, not an average of sentence scores.

The four precisions are then folded into one number:

$$\mathrm{BLEU} = \mathrm{BP}\cdot\exp\!\Big(\sum_{n=1}^{4}\tfrac{1}{4}\log p_n\Big),\qquad \mathrm{BP}=\min\!\big(1,\;e^{\,1-r/c}\big)$$

where $c$ is total candidate length and $r$ the matched reference length.

The brevity penalty exists because precision on its own has an obvious exploit. A system that emits only the single word it is most sure of scores a perfect precision on that word. BLEU never computes recall, so $\mathrm{BP}$ stands in for it: once the candidate corpus is shorter than $r$, the exponent $1 - r/c$ turns negative and the whole score is scaled down. Multiply what comes out by 100 to get the reported scale.

The exponentiated average of logs is a geometric mean, and that has one sharp consequence. If any single $p_n$ is zero, its log is $-\infty$ and the entire score collapses to zero. A $p_4$ of zero is easy to hit on one sentence, which is a second reason the metric is only computed corpus-wide.

Note what BLEU's input actually is. It is the decoded string — not the weights, not the output distribution. The score therefore moves with decoding choices as much as it moves with the model. The paper's numbers come from [[beam-search]] with beam 4, a [[length-penalty|length penalty $\alpha = 0.6$]], [[checkpoint-averaging|averaged checkpoints]], and a [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] vocabulary whose pieces have to be reassembled into words before a single n-gram is counted. Each of those is a knob on the reported number that is not the trained model.

### Why the paper reports it, and what it hides

Scoring emitted text rather than likelihood is exactly what lets BLEU disagree with [[perplexity]]. The clearest instance is [[label-smoothing|label smoothing]] at $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$. Smoothing trains the model to put less than full probability on the reference token, so by construction it ends up less confident there.

Perplexity is a function of precisely that probability, so perplexity gets worse. Accuracy and BLEU improve anyway. The paper states this flatly and does not explain it.

The reading that fits is that a smoothed model ranks candidate continuations better even though it is worse calibrated on the single gold token. BLEU only ever sees the ranking, by way of the string the search produced; perplexity only ever sees the calibration. That is an interpretation offered here, not an argument the paper makes.

BLEU also carries structural weight in the paper's case, not just its results. It is one of the two axes of [[table-2]]. The other axis is [[training-flops-estimate|estimated training FLOPs]], which is an estimate rather than a measured quantity. The claim the table is making is that the Transformer wins on both axes at once.

Evidence strength is not uniform across these numbers. The +2.0 English-to-German margin over prior work, ensembles included in the comparison, is well outside typical rerun noise.

The [[transformer-ablations|Table 3]] deltas are not. They run from [[attention-heads-ablation|0.9 BLEU for single-head attention]] down to 0.1 for [[learned-positional-embedding|learned positions]] in place of sinusoids. These are single runs, on the development set, with no seeds and no variance reported — which leaves nothing to hold a 0.1 gap up against.

And the paper is internally inconsistent on one of its own headline numbers. English-to-French appears as 41.0 in Section 6.1, and as 41.8 in both the abstract and [[table-2]].

Byte-pair encoding is the step that turns raw text into the integer sequence the model actually consumes. The model needs a closed vocabulary: a finite list of token ids, fixed before training begins. BPE gives one, and it gives one with a particular property — any string at all can be encoded in it, including words that never appeared in training. There is no unknown-token escape hatch, because none is needed.

The construction is a greedy loop over the training corpus. Split everything into individual characters. Count how often each adjacent pair of symbols occurs. Take the single most frequent pair and merge it into one new symbol, everywhere it appears. Then count pairs again over the rewritten corpus and repeat ([[bpe-merge-algorithm]]).

Every merge adds exactly one entry to the vocabulary. So the final vocabulary is the starting character set plus one entry per merge, which makes the number of merges the only real hyperparameter of the scheme ([[bpe-vocabulary-size]]). Nothing else has to be chosen.

New text is handled by replaying the same merges. Split the new string into characters, then apply the learned merge operations in the order they were learned ([[bpe-segmentation-at-test-time]]). A word the corpus never contained simply stops merging earlier and comes out as several known pieces.

Now the paper's actual setting. For [[wmt-2014-en-de|WMT 2014 English-German]], about 4.5M sentence pairs, the paper reports a single vocabulary of roughly 37000 tokens, shared between the source side and the target side.

Shared is a claim about how the merges were learned: over English and German text together, in one pass, rather than separately per language ([[joint-bpe-shared-vocabulary]]). The consequence is that one token id means the same string on both sides.

That consequence is what makes the rest of the setup coherent. A single embedding matrix of size $37000 \times 512$ — 37000 rows for the vocabulary, 512 columns because that is [[d-model|$d_{model}$]] — can fill three roles at once. It is the encoder input embedding, the decoder input embedding, and the pre-softmax projection ([[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing]]). None of that holds together if token id 1042 denotes different strings in the two languages.

The BPE token is also the unit of batching. A batch holds roughly 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens ([[length-based-batching]]). That is not a fixed sentence count, so the number of sentences in a batch moves with how long the tokenized sentences happen to be.

### What it costs

Subword segmentation is a trade, and the two sides of it pull against each other ([[vocabulary-vs-sequence-length-tradeoff]]). Fewer merges means a smaller vocabulary, and a smaller vocabulary means a smaller softmax to normalize over and a smaller embedding matrix to carry. But fewer merges also means finer pieces, so every sentence comes out as a longer token sequence.

Longer sequences are not free. Self-attention cost grows as $n^2 \cdot d$ in the sequence length $n$. Shrinking the vocabulary therefore buys cheaper embeddings and pays for them quadratically in attention. The choice of 37000 is a point on that curve, not a free win.

Section 4 leans on the short-sequence end of the same curve. Its comparison of layer types holds that self-attention is cheaper per layer than recurrence only when $n < d$ — only when a sentence has fewer tokens than the model has dimensions ([[complexity-per-layer]], [[table-1]]). For that argument to go through, the condition has to actually hold for real tokenized sentences. The paper's support for it is a pointer: byte-pair and [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] representations are what state-of-the-art translation models use.

### How strong the evidence is

Thin, and the paper does not claim otherwise.

No experiment isolates BPE. [[table-3]] is the one-knob-at-a-time study, and the knobs it turns are head count, $d_k$, depth, dropout, and [[positional-encoding]]. Vocabulary and tokenization are never among them.

Nor is there an accidental comparison to fall back on. [[wmt-2014-en-fr|English-French]] uses 32000 word pieces instead — but it is also a different language pair and a different dataset. The two schemes are never compared under matched conditions.

The $n < d$ claim has the same shape of gap. It is asserted in section 4 with a citation, and no table in the paper reports actual tokenized sentence lengths. The condition is argued, not measured.

What remains is a reading rather than a result. BPE here is an inherited, sensible default that the results are consistent with. It is not a tested design decision.

Constituency parsing takes a sentence and returns its syntactic tree. The words are grouped into nested labeled phrases: a noun phrase sitting inside a verb phrase, that verb phrase sitting inside a clause.

The paper does not run this task because it cares about parsing. It runs it as a transfer check. The question is whether a configuration tuned for translation can be pointed at a structurally different task with almost nothing changed.

### Turning a tree into a string

The [[transformer]] emits a flat token sequence and nothing else. A tree is not a flat sequence. So the tree has to be flattened before the model can be asked to produce one.

[[parse-tree-linearization]] does the flattening. It walks the tree depth-first, and on entering a node it emits an open-bracket token carrying that node's label. On leaving the node it emits a matching close token. The sentence's own words fall out in order at the leaves, wrapped in that bracket string.

Once the tree is a string, parsing is ordinary [[sequence-transduction]]. Sentence in, bracket string out. The same encoder-decoder shape that maps English to German maps a sentence to its parse.

Two things still make this unlike translation, and both come from the shape of the output.

The first is length. Every node in the tree contributes an open token and a close token on top of the words themselves, so the output runs several times longer than the input. A translation's output is roughly as long as its input. A linearized parse is not.

The second is that the output is not free-form. Brackets have to nest, and every bracket that opens has to close. The leaves have to be exactly the input words, in exactly the input order.

Nothing in the architecture enforces either constraint. There is no stack keeping track of open brackets, and no mechanism tying the leaves back to the source tokens. The decoder has to learn both from data.

The configuration is close to the translation model, with two deliberate changes. It uses 4 layers in each stack rather than the [[n-layers|six]] used for translation. And it sets $d_{model} = 1024$: the base [[d-model|model width]] is 512, so this is double it, and every sub-layer and embedding now outputs a 1024-dimensional vector.

There are two training regimes. The first is [[penn-treebank-wsj]] alone — about 40K hand-parsed sentences, with a 16K-token vocabulary. The second is [[semi-supervised-parsing]], which adds roughly 17M automatically parsed sentences on top of those and raises the vocabulary to 32K.

Both regimes follow the [[wsj-parsing-protocol]]: tune on Section 22, report on Section 23. That split is the standard one for this benchmark, so the numbers land next to published parsers rather than in isolation.

The list of things re-tuned for parsing is short. [[residual-dropout]] and [[attention-dropout]], the learning rate, and the beam size. Everything else carried over unchanged from the English-to-German base model. The shortness of that list is what the experiment is testing.

At inference, [[beam-search]] widens to 21, with a [[length-penalty|length penalty of $\alpha = 0.3$]]. The [[inference-length-limit|cap on output length]] goes to input length + 300 tokens. Both are concessions to the long, structured output: with a parse running several times the length of its input, a tighter cap would cut valid parses off before they finished closing their brackets.

### What the numbers support

[[table-4]] carries the entire claim. There is no other parsing evidence in the paper.

Take the WSJ-only setting first. The model reaches 91.3 F1. That is above every discriminative parser listed in the table except one: [[recurrent-neural-network-grammar|Dyer et al.'s RNNG]], at 91.7.

It is also above the [[berkeley-parser]], and that comparison is the load-bearing one. RNN sequence-to-sequence parsers had not previously beaten a classical grammar-based parser in the 40K-sentence regime. With that little training data, the grammar's built-in structure had been worth more than what a generic sequence model could learn from the trees alone.

Now the semi-supervised setting. With the ~17M extra machine-parsed sentences, the score goes to 92.7, the best semi-supervised row in the table.

Read the evidence as thin, though. There is one run per setting. No variance is reported. The margins separating neighbouring rows are a few tenths of an F1 point, and with a single run and no variance figure, nothing in the table establishes that a few tenths is a real gap rather than noise.

RNNG also still wins on WSJ-only, and it is worth being specific about what RNNG has that the Transformer does not. RNNG builds trees using explicit tree-structured operations, so the model's own computation mirrors the object it is producing. The Transformer has no such bias. It is the translation architecture with different tokens at each end.

So the generic architecture gets close to the task-specific model without the task-specific inductive bias. It does not get past it.

The paper's own summary is that the model does "surprisingly well", and it stops there. That is about the right strength for what one run per setting can support.

The decoder is the right-hand tower in [[fig-1]]: the half of the model that emits tokens.

It exists because the encoder, on its own, finishes nothing. The encoder reads the source sentence and hands back a set of representations $z = (z_1, \dots, z_n)$, one vector per input position. Those vectors are not an output sequence, and nothing in the encoder turns them into one. Something has to take $z$ and produce $(y_1, \dots, y_m)$, one symbol at a time. And it has to do that in a way that still trains in parallel, or the paper has given back the speed it just won.

Structurally the decoder is a copy of the [[encoder-stack]] with one thing added. Same depth: [[n-layers|$N=6$]] identical layers. Same wrapper around every [[sub-layer]] — the sub-layer's output is added back onto its own input and the sum is normalized, $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$, which is a [[residual-connection]] followed by [[layer-normalization]]. Same width everywhere: every sub-layer and every embedding emits vectors of size [[d-model|$d_{model}$]] $= 512$.

The addition is a third sub-layer. An encoder layer holds two; a decoder layer holds three, in a fixed order.

First [[masked-decoder-self-attention|masked self-attention]] over the output positions. Then [[encoder-decoder-attention|attention over the encoder output]]. Then the [[position-wise-feed-forward-network|feed-forward block]] of [[eq-ffn]], which takes each position's vector on its own and pushes it through 512 → [[d-ff|2048]] → ReLU → 512.

The shapes are worth holding onto, so here is what each of those three sub-layers is actually handed.

Input to layer 1 is an $m \times 512$ matrix. The rows are the output embeddings shifted right by one position, with [[positional-encoding]] added.

The masked self-attention sub-layer is ordinary [[multi-head-attention]], with the base model's usual split: [[num-heads-h|$h = 8$]] heads dividing the 512 model dimensions between them, so each head works in $512/8 = 64$ dimensions, giving [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = 64$]]. One thing changes inside [[eq-attention]]. Before the softmax, the score for every position later in the sequence than the query is set to $-\infty$, which is [[causal-masking]]. Exponentiating $-\infty$ gives zero, so those positions get exactly zero weight. The result is that the $m \times m$ matrix of attention weights is lower-triangular.

The cross-attention sub-layer mixes its sources. Queries come from the decoder — $m \times 64$ per head. Keys and values come from the encoder's final output — $n \times 64$ per head. Dotting $m$ queries against $n$ keys gives an $m \times n$ attention matrix, and this one carries no mask at all: every output position may look at every input position. Note also that there is one encoder output, computed once, and the same matrix feeds the cross-attention of all six decoder layers.

### What the mask buys and what it costs

The mask and the one-position shift work as a pair. The shift means the vector sitting in slot $i$ of the decoder input is the embedding of output token $i-1$. The mask means slot $i$ cannot attend to slots $i+1$ and beyond. Put together, the prediction made at position $i$ has been exposed only to outputs before $i$ — the [[auto-regressive-generation|auto-regressive]] property the training loss assumes.

The payoff is that this restriction costs nothing at training time. All $m$ positions go through the stack in a single pass, because the mask enforces the ordering rather than the computation order enforcing it. That is the whole point of dropping recurrence.

The cost lands at inference instead. Generation is still strictly sequential there: token $i$ has to exist before it can be fed in as input for token $i+1$, so decoding is one forward pass per token, $m$ of them. [[beam-search]] multiplies that count further.

The decoder is also the more expensive of the two towers. It runs three sub-layers per layer where the encoder runs two, and each layer's cross-attention adds $O(n \cdot m \cdot d)$ work on top.

### How well is this supported

Thinly, if you want the decoder's design isolated from everything else.

[[fig-1]] shows the arrangement, but a diagram is a description, not a measurement — nothing here measures the decoder. [[table-3]] varies head count, $d_k$, dropout and layer count, but it varies them across the whole model. No row removes the cross-attention sub-layer. No row gives the encoder and the decoder different depths.

[[table-4]] does use a 4-layer variant, for parsing rather than translation. That is evidence that $N=6$ is not sacred; it is not evidence that six is the right number for the decoder.

So treat the decoder's shape as an inherited design that the paper kept, rather than a choice it defended with numbers.

pages.body:
The encoder-decoder split is the one part of the design the paper inherits rather than proposes. Every competitive [[sequence-transduction|sequence transduction]] model of the time already had this shape: one half reads the whole source, the other half writes the target while consulting what the first half produced. That was true of the recurrent models and equally true of the convolutional ones. The paper keeps the shape and swaps out what the two halves are built from.

It is here first because it is the frame. The attention math only makes sense once you know which vectors are flowing where.

Start with the encoder. It takes $n$ input symbols and emits $z = (z_1, \dots, z_n)$ — one vector per input position, not one vector for the sentence as a whole. Each of those vectors has width $d_{model} = 512$, the model's [[d-model|shared width]]. So the encoder's output is an $n \times 512$ matrix: one row per input token, 512 numbers per row.

That shape is worth pausing on. A longer input produces more rows, not a more crowded summary. Nothing is squeezed through a fixed-size bottleneck on the way out of the encoder.

The decoder then emits $(y_1, \dots, y_m)$. The length $m$ is free — it is not tied to $n$ in any way. Output length is decided by the decoder as it generates, not fixed in advance by how long the input happened to be.

Both halves have the same internal shape: a stack of $N = 6$ identical layers ([[encoder-stack]], [[decoder-stack]]).

### Where the two halves touch

There is exactly one channel between the two stacks, and it is [[encoder-decoder-attention]]. That sub-layer takes its queries from the decoder, and it takes its keys and values from the encoder's final output.

Two details in that sentence do real work. First, it is the encoder's *final* output — the encoder runs to completion before the decoder consults it. Second, the same $n \times 512$ matrix is handed to all six decoder layers. Decoder layer 6 reads exactly what decoder layer 1 reads; there is no per-layer pairing between the stacks.

Cut that channel and you are left with two unrelated language models.

The other two attention sites stay inside their own half. [[encoder-self-attention]] runs over all $n$ positions with no masking at all, so every input position can gather from every other. [[masked-decoder-self-attention]] is the same operation under a restriction: it uses [[causal-masking]], which sets the scores for future positions to $-\infty$ before the softmax, so those positions come out with zero weight. The effect is that position $i$ cannot see position $i+1$.

That mask is what makes [[auto-regressive-generation]] trainable in parallel. During training the whole target sequence is fed in at once, and all $m$ positions are computed in a single pass. The ordering constraint is still enforced — but by the mask, not by a loop.

At inference there is no such trick, because the tokens do not exist yet. To produce token $t$ you need the tokens before it as input, and token $t-1$ was itself produced by the step before. So you run $m$ sequential steps, one per token, each conditioned on what was already emitted.

### What it costs

The paper's parallelism claim is narrower than it first sounds. It is about computation within a training example. Generation itself is still strictly step-by-step, and the conclusion lists making generation less sequential as future work rather than as something solved here.

The second cost follows from taking recurrence out. A recurrent model knows the order of its tokens because it walks them in order — the order is in the procedure. Attention has no such walk. Each output of a self-attention layer is a weighted sum over all positions, and those weights come from the contents of the vectors being compared, not from where those vectors sit in the sequence.

So nothing in either stack knows what order its tokens are in. Position has to be put back by hand, at the inputs — see [[eq-posenc]].

[[fig-1]] is the map for all of this. Read it as a schematic, though: it fixes the wiring, not the sizes.

And no experiment isolates this choice. The frame is held constant across every result reported — [[table-2]] and [[table-3]] measure what fills the two halves, not the split itself.

pages.body:
The encoder's job is to turn a source sentence of $n$ tokens into $n$ vectors, each one 512 wide. It computes all $n$ of them at once, rather than producing one position and then the next.

The reason the model needs such a component at all comes from the [[encoder-decoder-architecture|encoder-decoder frame]]. The decoder has to have a fixed memory to read from while it generates. That memory is the encoder's final output.

[[encoder-decoder-attention]] takes its keys and its values from that output and from nothing else. So no decoder layer has anything to attend over until the whole encoder stack has finished running. The encoder runs once; the decoder reads the same result at every layer and every step.

### What actually runs

Start with what goes in. Each token is looked up in a table of [[token-embeddings]], and a [[positional-encoding]] vector is added to that embedding. Dropout is applied to the sum. What comes out is an $n \times 512$ matrix — one row per token, 512 columns per row.

That matrix then passes through six identical layers ([[n-layers|$N = 6$]]). Identical in structure, not in weights. Each layer contains two [[sub-layer|sub-layers]], and both are wrapped the same way:

$$x \leftarrow \mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$$

Read that as three steps in order. Run the sub-layer on $x$, add the original $x$ back to the result, then normalize the sum.

Sub-layer one is [[multi-head-attention]] used as [[self-attention]]. Self-attention here means the queries, the keys and the values are all the same tensor: the previous layer's output. Position $i$ forms a query from its own vector, scores that query against the key at every position, and takes a weighted sum of the values.

No mask is applied at this point. Position $i$ therefore attends over all $n$ positions, the ones behind it and the ones ahead of it alike. That missing mask is the only thing that separates this sub-layer from the decoder's version of it.

Sub-layer two is the [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]] of [[eq-ffn|equation (2)]]. It is applied to each row of the matrix on its own. Row $i$ is transformed without reference to any other row.

Shapes never change anywhere in the stack. Every sub-layer takes $n \times 512$ and returns $n \times 512$, so every layer does too, and so does the stack as a whole.

Weights are shared across positions but not across layers. The same feed-forward matrices are applied to all $n$ rows, but layer two shares nothing with layer one except its shape. Six layers with two sub-layers each makes twelve sub-layers and twelve separate parameter sets: roughly 1M parameters in the attention projections and 2M in the feed-forward net, per layer.

[[residual-dropout|Dropout at $p=0.1$]] is applied to each sub-layer's output, before that output is added back to $x$.

### Why this width, and what it costs

[[residual-connection|Residual connections]] force the width to be constant. The addition of $x$ to $\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$ is elementwise, and it only makes sense if the two have the same shape. So the paper pins [[d-model|$d_{model}=512$]] across every sub-layer and every embedding layer.

That one constraint propagates downward into the pieces. Multi-head attention has to divide the 512 dimensions among [[num-heads-h|eight heads]]: $512/8 = 64$, so each head operates in [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = 64$]] dimensions. The feed-forward net widens each position's vector to [[d-ff|2048]] internally, and that widening has to be undone — projected back down to 512 — before the block returns anything to the residual stream.

[[layer-normalization]] closes each wrapper. It rescales each position's vector using only that vector's own features, not the other positions and not the rest of the batch.

That is the shape of the design. The cost side is attention that grows quadratically: relating every position to every other position is $n^2$ score computations, which comes to $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ per layer.

The paper accepts that cost on the argument laid out in [[table-1]], rather than on a measurement.

### How strong the evidence is

[[fig-1]] shows the left tower and settles the wiring. Which sub-layer feeds which, and where the residual paths run, is not in doubt.

For what the layers actually learn, the paper offers only pictures. [[fig-5]], [[fig-3]] and [[fig-4]] are all drawn from [[encoder-self-attention|encoder self-attention]] at layer 5 of 6, and the text says the patterns "seem related" to sentence structure. Nothing in those figures is quantified.

The depth of six is stated, not defended. The [[table-3|ablations]] vary heads, key size, dropout and model size, and Section 6.2 concludes only that bigger models are better.

pages.body:
The paper trains with label smoothing at $\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$. It cites [36] for the method and gives it two sentences in Section 5.4. That is the entire treatment.

Label smoothing sits in the [[transformer-training-recipe|recipe]] as one of three kinds of [[regularization]]. The other two are [[residual-dropout|residual dropout]], which acts during training, and [[checkpoint-averaging|checkpoint averaging]], which acts at decode time.

### The operation

Start at the output end of the decoder. At every output position it emits a vector of logits, one entry per token in the shared [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] vocabulary — about 37000 tokens for the English-German runs. [[softmax]] turns that vector into a distribution $p$ over those 37000 tokens.

Training normally minimizes cross entropy between $p$ and a one-hot target. One-hot means all the probability mass on the single reference token and exactly zero on everything else. Smoothing replaces that target with a mixture, which is the definition given in the cited work ([[label-smoothing-regularization|LSR]]):

$$q'(k) = (1-\epsilon_{ls})\,\delta_{k,y} + \epsilon_{ls}\,u(k)$$

Put the paper's numbers into it. The prior $u$ is uniform and $\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$, so the true token $y$ is asked for $1 - 0.1 = 0.9$ instead of $1$. The remaining $0.1$ is spread evenly across the vocabulary, which gives each of the other roughly 37000 tokens a target of $0.1/37000 \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-6}$.

Cross entropy is linear in the target, so substituting the mixture splits the loss into two pieces that add. The first is the ordinary one-hot cross entropy. The second is a term that pulls the predicted distribution toward $u$, scaled by $\epsilon_{ls}$ — see [[lsr-as-two-cross-entropy-losses]].

The gradient changes accordingly. At logit $k$ it becomes $p_k - q'(k)$, where before it was $p_k - \delta_{k,y}$. The only thing that moved is what $p$ is being compared against, but that is enough to move where training comes to rest.

Consider the one-hot case first. At the correct logit the gradient is $p_y - 1$, which is zero only when $p_y$ reaches exactly $1$. Softmax approaches $1$ only as the correct logit runs away from all the others, so there is always some remaining pressure to push it further ([[overconfidence-and-bounded-logit-gradient]]).

Under smoothing the fixed point is finite. Gradients vanish when $p$ matches $q'$, which asks for a ratio of $0.9$ to $2.7 \times 10^{-6}$ between the correct probability and each other one — a factor of roughly 333000. In logit space that is $\ln(0.9/2.7\times10^{-6}) \approx 12.7$. So the correct logit settles about 12.7 above the rest rather than growing without bound.

Nothing in the forward pass changes. Same $d_{model}=512$, same weights, same shapes. Only the target tensor is different.

LSR has two knobs: the smoothing parameter $\epsilon_{ls}$ and the choice of prior $u$ ([[smoothing-parameter-epsilon]]). The paper reports only the single setting $0.1$ with uniform $u$, and never sweeps it.

### The trade it makes

[[perplexity]] gets worse, and mechanically it must. Perplexity is the exponentiated negative log-probability the model assigns to the reference tokens. A model trained to hold back a tenth of its mass assigns those tokens less probability, so the number goes up.

The floor this creates is easy to see. Take a model that reproduced its smoothed target exactly, putting $0.9$ on the reference token every time. Its per-token perplexity would still sit near $1/0.9$, purely from the mass it was told to withhold.

[[bleu]] moves the other way, and the reason is what happens at decode time. [[beam-search]] compares candidate continuations against each other and keeps the best ones. It reads the ranking of candidates, not the absolute probability the model puts on the reference. A change that costs probability mass therefore need not cost rank.

The paper accepts the perplexity cost on those grounds and says so in one line: it "hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score."

That claim is asserted, not demonstrated. [[table-3]] is the one place the paper reports development perplexity and BLEU side by side for each configuration, so it is where the two metrics moving in opposite directions would be visible.

But its rows vary head count, $d_k$, model size, [[size-and-dropout-ablation|dropout]] and [[positional-encoding]]. None of them turns smoothing off. Section 6.2's prose walks through dropout and never mentions smoothing at all.

So the headline numbers reported in [[table-2]] were all trained with $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$. How much of those numbers label smoothing is worth is not something this paper measures.

pages.body:
Section 4 makes the paper's case for [[self-attention]] before a single experiment runs. It is an argument from cost and structure, not from results.

The section starts by fixing one task so that different layer types can be compared on equal terms. Take a sequence $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ and map it to another sequence $(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ of the same length, with $x_i, z_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$. That is exactly the job of one hidden layer inside an encoder or a decoder, so any candidate layer type can be dropped into the slot and scored.

Three axes do the scoring. The first is [[complexity-per-layer|how much arithmetic one layer performs]]. The second is [[minimum-sequential-operations|how much of that arithmetic must run in order]], one step waiting on the last, rather than all at once. The third is [[maximum-path-length|how far a signal has to travel between any two positions]] — counting the steps in the network a value at position $i$ must pass through before it can influence the output at position $j$.

The third axis is the one carrying the argument. The paper's claim is that [[long-range-dependencies]] are easier to learn when the forward signal and the backward gradient cross fewer steps, and it cites Hochreiter et al. for that link.

Self-attention makes the path as short as it can be. Every position attends directly to every other position in one operation, so any two positions are neighbours and the path length is 1 no matter how large $n$ gets.

A [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent]] layer is the opposite case. Its hidden state at position $t$ is a function of the hidden state at position $t-1$, so to get position 5 you must first have position 4, and to get that you must first have position 3. That chain is $O(n)$ operations long, and none of its links can be computed in parallel with the others.

This is the [[sequential-computation-bottleneck|one dependency chain doing two kinds of damage]]. It is what blocks parallelism within a training example, and it is also the path a gradient has to walk back down, so both the compute cost and the learning difficulty come from the same structure.

### The numbers

[[table-1]] is where this framework stops being a claim and becomes concrete. Without the table, Section 4 is three assertions.

Take the per-layer arithmetic first. Self-attention costs $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, because every one of $n$ positions scores against every other across $d$ dimensions. Recurrence costs $O(n \cdot d^2)$: one matrix multiply of size $d \times d$ per position. Convolution costs $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ for kernel width $k$.

Compare the first two directly. Set $n^2 \cdot d$ against $n \cdot d^2$ and divide both by $n \cdot d$, and what is left is $n$ against $d$. So self-attention is the cheaper layer exactly when $n < d$. The paper argues this is the usual case for sentence-level translation, where sentences tokenized with [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] or [[byte-pair-encoding|byte-pair]] vocabularies are shorter than the model width of $d = 512$ ([[d-model]]).

The second axis is quicker. Self-attention and convolution both need $O(1)$ sequential operations — the whole layer is one batched matrix computation. Recurrence needs $O(n)$, for the reason above.

[[convolutional-sequence-models|Convolutional]] layers lose on the third axis, and they lose differently from recurrence. A single convolutional layer with $k < n$ does not connect all pairs of positions at all, because a position only sees the $k$ positions inside its kernel window. Connecting the whole sequence takes a stack: $O(n/k)$ layers with ordinary convolutions, or $O(\log_k n)$ layers with [[dilated-convolutions]], which space the kernel taps apart so each layer covers a wider span.

Cost is the other half of the convolution story. [[separable-convolutions]] cut the per-layer cost to $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$. Push $k$ all the way to $n$, the most expensive setting, and that becomes $O(n^2 \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$ — which is self-attention plus a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network|point-wise feed-forward layer]]. That combination is the paper's own layer. So the cheapest convolutional variant, at its widest kernel, only matches what the Transformer already does.

### What it costs, and how strong the evidence is

The $n^2$ term is the price of the short path. Every position scoring against every position is what makes path length 1, and it is also what makes the layer expensive once sequences get long.

For long sequences, then, self-attention is the expensive option rather than the cheap one. The paper's answer to this is a sketch, not a result: [[restricted-self-attention|have each position attend only to a neighbourhood of size $r$]], which cuts the cost but gives up the constant path, raising it to $O(n/r)$. The paper says it plans to investigate this in future work. No experiment in this paper backs it.

The evidence behind Table 1 needs the same care. The table is asymptotic analysis, not measurement — there are no wall-clock timings in it, and no experiment isolates path length from everything else that changed at the same time.

That limit matters for how the results should be read. The BLEU numbers in [[table-2]] show that the architecture works. They do not show that short paths are the reason it works.

The interpretability observation at the end of the section ([[fig-3]], [[fig-4]], [[fig-5]]) sits in the same category. It is offered as a side benefit rather than as support for the main argument, and it is qualitative.

pages.body:
The learning rate in this paper is not a constant that you tune once and then leave alone. It is a function of the step number. Every step of training computes its own value from the step count.

Section 5.3 writes that function down as [[eq-lrate|Equation (3)]]:

$$lrate = d_{model}^{-0.5} \cdot \min(step\_num^{-0.5},\ step\_num \cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5})$$

This is the number handed to [[adam-optimizer|Adam]] each step. It arrives before Adam does anything of its own. The schedule sets the overall size of the update, and Adam's per-parameter rescaling then divides that size up across the individual weights.

The shape of the curve comes entirely from the $\min$. Take its two arguments one at a time. Early in training $step\_num$ is small, so the second argument, $step\_num \cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5}$, is small and rising, while the first argument $step\_num^{-0.5}$ is large. The $\min$ therefore returns the second one, which grows linearly in the step number.

Later the situation reverses. The linear term keeps climbing, the $step\_num^{-0.5}$ term keeps shrinking, and the $\min$ switches to the shrinking one.

The switch happens at a specific place. Setting $step\_num^{-0.5} = step\_num \cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5}$ gives $step\_num^{1.5} = warmup\_steps^{1.5}$, so the two branches cross exactly at $step\_num = warmup\_steps$. The whole schedule is one linear ramp up followed by an inverse-square-root decay, with the peak sitting at that crossover.

### The actual numbers

Start with the factor sitting outside the $\min$. With [[d-model|$d_{model} = 512$]], that factor is $512^{-0.5} = 1/\sqrt{512} \approx 0.0442$. It multiplies everything else in the formula, so it is a fixed scale on the entire curve rather than something that changes over training.

Now the ramp. With [[warmup-steps-4000|$warmup\_steps = 4000$]], the warmup branch is $step\_num$ multiplied by the constant $0.0442 \cdot 4000^{-1.5}$. That constant works out to about $1.7 \times 10^{-7}$, and it is the same increment added at every step of warmup.

So the rate starts at roughly zero and climbs in a straight line. By step 4000 it has accumulated 4000 of those increments, which puts the peak near $7 \times 10^{-4}$.

After the peak the decay takes over, and it is gradual. The rate is about $1.4 \times 10^{-4}$ at step 100{,}000, which is where the base model stops. It is about $8 \times 10^{-5}$ at step 300{,}000, which is where the big model stops — see [[training-hardware-and-schedule|the training schedule]] for those step counts.

Those step counts also tell you how much of training the warmup actually covers. Four thousand steps out of 100{,}000 is the first 4% of base training. Four thousand out of 300{,}000 is the first ~1.3% of big training.

The ramp is the part everyone talks about, but it is the short part. The decay is what the model spends nearly all of its steps under.

The $d_{model}^{-0.5}$ factor is the part that is easy to skip over, and it is doing something the rest of the formula is not. Every other term in the equation is about where you are in the run. That factor is about the model you are training.

Widen the model and $d_{model}^{-0.5}$ shrinks, so every step of the schedule gets proportionally smaller, with no retuning of the schedule itself. The learning rate is tied to the architecture rather than to the run. That matters here because the paper trains [[base-vs-big-transformer|two sizes]] and uses the same formula for both.

### What the paper does and does not show

The paper states the schedule and moves on. There is no derivation of it.

There is also no ablation of it. No curve of BLEU against $warmup\_steps$, no comparison against a constant learning rate, no comparison against a step decay.

The other experiments do not fill that gap either. The [[table-3|Table 3 ablations]] vary the number of heads, $d_k$, depth, dropout and the positional encodings, and they hold this optimizer setup fixed throughout. Nothing in the paper isolates the schedule's contribution.

The headline results are in the same position. The [[table-2|Table 2]] BLEU numbers all come from runs that used this schedule, so they say nothing about what it contributed on its own. Treat it as a reported recipe, not a measured result.

One thing the section does make explicit is that the schedule and the optimizer settings were chosen together. Alongside the schedule the paper sets [[transformer-adam-settings|$\beta_2 = 0.98$]], rather than the usual 0.999.

That change has a direct effect on Adam's behaviour. $\beta_2$ controls the decay of the running average of squared gradients, so a lower value makes that second-moment estimate forget older gradients faster and adapt more quickly when the gradient scale changes. The paper offers no reason for either choice — not for the value of $\beta_2$, and not for the schedule.

There is a standard story about why warmup helps: Adam's moment estimates are built from very few samples over the first handful of steps and are unreliable there, and a randomly initialised network produces large, noisy gradients that a full-size step would follow too far. That argument is not in this paper.

It is inference, not something Section 5.3 claims. What the paper does hand you is a reproducible piece of the [[transformer-training-recipe|training recipe]], with every constant filled in.

Multi-head attention is the wrapper the Transformer puts around [[scaled-dot-product-attention]]. The unwrapped version would run a single attention function over the full-width vectors the model carries everywhere else, which are [[d-model|$d_{model}=512$]] dimensions wide. Multi-head attention does something else instead. It runs $h$ attention functions side by side, each on its own narrower learned projection of the same input, then stitches their outputs back together at the end.

The paper gives one reason for the wrapper, in Section 2 and again in 3.2.2. Attention does not pick out a position; it returns a weighted *average* over all of them. An average is a blend, and once positions are blended there is no way to read back what any single one of them contributed ([[attention-averaging-resolution-cost]]). That is the resolution being spent.

Several heads are the way around it. Each head projects the input differently, so each is reading a different representation subspace, and the heads can attend to different positions at the same time. With a single head, the paper says, "averaging inhibits this."

### The operation

Start with an input of $n$ positions, $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 512}$. A head never sees $X$ at full width. Three learned matrices ([[attention-projection-matrices]]) cut it down to 64 dimensions first: $W^Q_i, W^K_i \in \mathbb{R}^{512 \times 64}$ and $W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{512 \times 64}$, one set per head $i$.

Feed those three projections to [[eq-attention|Equation (1)]], unchanged from the single-head case. What comes back is one [[attention-head|head]]'s output: $n$ positions, 64 dimensions each.

Now do that $h=8$ times ([[num-heads-h]]), each head with its own three matrices. Concatenate the eight $n \times 64$ outputs along the feature axis and the width is back to $n \times 512$. Apply one final learned matrix, $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{512 \times 512}$, to mix the heads together. That is all [[eq-multihead|the MultiHead equation]] says.

The right panel of [[fig-2]] draws the same steps as data flow: the split into parallel blocks, then the concat, then the final linear. Those last two are the ones worth checking against the picture. The `Concat` notation on its own does not make it obvious that a learned projection follows the concatenation.

The width of 64 is not arbitrary, and it is what keeps eight heads affordable. $d_{model}$ is 512, there are 8 heads, and each head gets an equal share of the width: $512/8 = 64$. Hence [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = 64$]].

Count the attention scores under that choice. Each head builds an $n \times n$ score matrix, and each entry costs $d_k$ multiply-adds, so all $h$ heads together cost $h \cdot n^2 d_k$. But $h \cdot d_k$ is $d_{model}$ by construction, so the total is $n^2 d_{model}$ — exactly what one head attending at full width would have cost.

The parameters land in the same place. Stack the eight $512 \times 64$ query matrices side by side and you have a single $512 \times 512$ matrix; the same holds for the key and value matrices, and $W^O$ is $512 \times 512$ already. Four matrices, $4 \times 512^2$ parameters, which is what one full-width head plus its output projection would have taken.

Heads are a reshape, not an extra budget line.

That is how they are implemented, too. Nobody loops over eight heads: stack the per-head matrices into one $512 \times 512$ projection, apply it once, reshape the result to $(n, 8, 64)$, and batch the attention over the head axis.

Every attention sub-layer in the model is this same block. The only things that vary between them are where $Q$, $K$, and $V$ come from, and whether a mask is applied to the scores. That covers all three uses: [[encoder-self-attention]], [[masked-decoder-self-attention]], and [[encoder-decoder-attention]].

### How strong is the evidence

For the wrapper itself, there is one number. Row (A) of [[table-3]] varies $h$ with total computation held fixed, so the comparison is between arrangements of the same compute, not between a bigger model and a smaller one. In that row, single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting. Raising $h$ too far hurts as well, because each head is then left with too few dimensions to work in ([[attention-heads-ablation]]).

That is a real ablation. It is also a single dev-set sweep on one language pair. And what it supports is "some heads help" — not the subspace story that motivated the design.

The subspace story rests on pictures. [[fig-3]], [[fig-4]], and [[fig-5]] show heads attending to visibly different things. The sharpest case is [[fig-4]]: head 5 and head 6 both attend from the word *its*, and the two of them resolve it to different antecedents.

The paper's own wording stays careful about what that shows ([[attention-interpretability]]). Heads "appear" to learn different tasks. Patterns "seem related" to sentence structure. Nothing there is measured.
