pages.body:
A positional encoding is a vector added to each token embedding at the very bottom of the [[encoder-stack]] and the [[decoder-stack]]. It carries nothing about the token itself. All it carries is which slot in the sequence that token sits in.

It is there because [[self-attention]] is order-blind. Attention scores every position against every other position, and nothing anywhere in that computation asks where either of them sat. Permute the input positions and the outputs come out permuted the same way, otherwise unchanged.

A [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent model]] never has this problem. It consumes position 1, then position 2, then position 3, so order is already baked into the order of the computation. The Transformer has no recurrence and no convolution, so nothing inside it supplies that signal. The encoding is the patch for what was removed.

### The operation

Build a matrix $PE$ of shape $n \times d_{model}$, where $n$ is the sequence length and [[d-model|$d_{model} = 512$]]. Row $pos$ is the vector for whatever token is at position $pos$. That row depends only on the integer $pos$, never on the identity of the token.

[[eq-posenc|Equation 3.5]] fills the matrix in. Even dimensions get $\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})$, and odd dimensions get the matching cosine. Because the slots pair up that way, a 512-wide row is really 256 sine/cosine pairs, each pair oscillating at its own frequency.

The exponent $2i/d_{model}$ is what sets those frequencies. It runs from $0$ at the first pair up toward $1$ at the last, so the wavelengths climb geometrically from $2\pi$ at one end to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ at the other. The low pairs flip quickly from one position to the next; the high pairs barely move across a whole sentence. See [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding]] for what that bank of frequencies looks like.

Then add — do not concatenate. The [[token-embeddings|embedding]] lookup comes first, [[sqrt-dmodel-embedding-multiplier|scaled by $\sqrt{d_{model}}$]]. That scaling matters here, because the two things being combined are on different footings: sinusoid entries are locked into $[-1,1]$ by construction, while embedding entries are whatever training makes them. Multiplying the embedding up by $\sqrt{d_{model}}$ keeps content from being swamped by position.

The row of $PE$ is added to that scaled embedding. Then [[residual-dropout|dropout]] at $p=0.1$ is applied to the sum.

That sum is the input to layer 1. Position is injected exactly once, right there at the bottom. Every one of the six layers above sees position only through whatever survives the [[residual-connection|residual stream]]. [[fig-1]] shows the same thing from the outside: in either tower, the foot of the stack is the only place anything positional enters the model.

### Why sinusoids, and how thin the evidence is

The paper gives two reasons for choosing fixed sinusoids over learned vectors, and it hedges the first of them.

The first reason is relative position. The authors "hypothesized" that sinusoids let the model attend by offset rather than by absolute slot. The property behind that guess is that for any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ — shifting by $k$ rotates each sine/cosine pair by a fixed angle, the same rotation at every $pos$. A linear map inside the model could therefore, in principle, implement "look $k$ positions back". See [[relative-position-linearity]]. The word "hypothesized" is the paper's own, and nothing downstream upgrades it.

The second reason is length. A sinusoid is defined at every position, so a fixed function may extrapolate to sequences longer than any seen in training. A per-position lookup table cannot do that at all: if training never reached a given position, that table has no row there to use.

Neither reason is tested.

What is tested is row (E) of [[table-3]]. That row swaps the sinusoids out for [[learned-positional-embedding|learned position vectors]] and reports "nearly identical results". Read for what it actually establishes, the ablation shows that the slot has to be filled by something. It does not show that sinusoids fill it better than the alternative does.

The extrapolation argument gets no comparable check. It remains a stated motivation, with no length-generalization experiment behind it.

The choice to add rather than concatenate has a cost of its own, and that cost is not measured either. Position and content share all 512 dimensions instead of each getting a private block of them. Whatever separating the two requires, the model has to do it from a single sum.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

pages.body:
The Transformer uses attention in three places. There is [[encoder-self-attention|self-attention inside the encoder]], [[masked-decoder-self-attention|masked self-attention inside the decoder]], and [[encoder-decoder-attention|attention from the decoder onto the encoder's output]]. Drawn in the architecture diagram they look like three separate mechanisms.

They are not. All three are calls to a single function, with different matrices passed in.

That function is what this page is about. It has two parts: a [[compatibility-function|compatibility function]] that scores how well a query matches a key, and the weighted sum over values that those scores then drive. The paper gives the combination a name, "scaled dot-product attention," because two attention variants were already in circulation at the time and this one is not quite either of them.

### The operation, with shapes

The shapes are what make the equation readable, so start there.

Pack the [[queries-keys-values|queries]] for a whole sequence into a matrix $Q$ of shape $n \times d_k$ — one row per query position. Pack the keys into $K$, of shape $m \times d_k$, and the values into $V$, of shape $m \times d_v$. Keys and values come in pairs, so both have $m$ rows; only their widths differ.

With those shapes fixed, [[eq-attention|Equation (1)]] is:

$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Take it one factor at a time.

$QK^{T}$ multiplies an $n \times d_k$ matrix by a $d_k \times m$ one, so the result is $n \times m$. Entry $(i, j)$ is query $i$ dotted with key $j$. That is one score for every query-key pair in the sequence, computed in a single matrix multiplication.

Every entry of that matrix is then divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$. This is the "scaled" in the name, and the reason for it is the subject of [[sqrt-dk-scaling|the second half of this page]].

Next comes the [[softmax]], applied along the key axis. Each of the $n$ rows becomes a distribution over the $m$ keys: all weights non-negative, each row summing to one.

Finally, multiply that $n \times m$ weight matrix by $V$, which is $m \times d_v$. The output is $n \times d_v$ — one vector per query. Because each row of weights is non-negative and sums to one, each output vector is a convex combination of the rows of $V$.

Now notice what is *not* in any of this: there are no learned weights. The function is two matrix multiplications and a softmax, and nothing inside it is trained.

The projections that produce $Q$, $K$, and $V$ do have parameters, but they sit outside this function, in [[multi-head-attention]]. That is also where the widths get set. $d_{model}$ is [[d-model|512]], and the base model runs [[num-heads-h|$h = 8$]] copies of the attention function in parallel, so each copy gets $512 / 8 = 64$ dimensions: [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = 64$]] per head, rather than one single copy running at the full 512.

One more thing happens inside this function that the equation does not show. [[causal-masking]] sets the forbidden entries of the pre-softmax score matrix to $-\infty$, which drives their softmax weights to zero. The left panel of [[fig-2]] draws the operation box by box and shows exactly where the mask sits in the chain.

### Why this scoring rule, and what it costs

Two questions follow from the definition. Why score with a dot product at all, and what does that choice give up?

The alternative on the table was [[additive-attention]], which scores each query-key pair with a small feed-forward network with one hidden layer. The paper's argument against it is not about accuracy. It says the two are similar in theoretical complexity, but that dot products are much faster and more space-efficient in practice, because the whole computation collapses into matrix multiplication — and matmul kernels are already heavily optimized.

That is the entire performance argument. The paper gives no timing table to back it up.

The scaling factor is the only thing separating this function from plain [[dot-product-attention]], and the paper's reasoning for it is explicitly hedged. The starting observation is a report from elsewhere: additive attention had been found to outperform unscaled dot products at larger $d_k$.

The authors *suspect* the cause is that the dot products grow large in magnitude as $d_k$ grows, pushing the softmax into a region where its gradients are extremely small.

The support for that suspicion is a variance argument in a footnote, resting on an independence assumption. It is not a measurement. Nor is there an ablation: no row of [[table-3]] removes the $\sqrt{d_k}$ factor to see what happens.

The cost of a scorer with no parameters shows up in [[key-size-ablation|rows (B)]] of [[table-3]]. Shrinking $d_k$ lowers BLEU.

The paper reads that as a hint — its word is a suggestion, not a conclusion — that a dot product may be too simple a compatibility function.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

pages.body:
Self-attention is the [[attention-mechanism|attention function]] run on a single sequence. The queries, the keys and the values are not drawn from three different places — they are all read off the same set of vectors. In the [[transformer|Transformer]], that set is the output of the previous layer of the same stack.

It is in the model because nothing else is. Recurrence has been removed, and so has convolution. That leaves self-attention as the only route by which one position's representation can come to depend on another's.

### The operation

Start with the previous layer's output $X$. Its shape is $n \times d_{model}$, where $n$ is the sequence length and $d_{model} = 512$. Every layer in the stack hands the next one a matrix of exactly this shape.

The work happens inside each of the $h=8$ heads of [[multi-head-attention|multi-head attention]]. A head begins with three learned projections of $X$: $Q = XW^Q$, $K = XW^K$, $V = XW^V$. Each of the three comes out $n \times 64$.

That 64 is not a free choice. The head dimensions are tied to the model width by [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h$]]: $d_{model}$ is 512, there are 8 heads, and $512/8 = 64$. So the eight heads split the width between them rather than each getting the full 512.

Now [[eq-attention|the attention equation]], one step at a time. First $QK^\top$, an $n \times n$ matrix whose entry in row $i$, column $j$ is the dot product of position $i$'s query with position $j$'s key — every position scored against every position, including itself. Those scores are divided by [[sqrt-dk-scaling|$\sqrt{d_k}$]]. Then a softmax runs along each row, so row $i$ becomes a distribution over all $n$ positions.

Multiplying that matrix by $V$ finishes the head. Each output row is a weighted average of the rows of $V$, with the weights taken from the corresponding row of the softmax.

The eight heads each produce an $n \times 64$ output. Concatenating them gives $n \times 512$ again, and projecting that through $W^O$ returns an $n \times d_{model}$ matrix. Same shape in, same shape out. That is the property that lets the layers stack.

Two consequences fall straight out of $Q$, $K$ and $V$ sharing a source, and both of them shape the rest of the architecture.

The first is about order. A score between two positions is a dot product of vectors computed from content alone — nothing in the expression refers to where either position sits in the sequence. Permute the input rows and the same set of scores comes back, merely permuted with them. The layer therefore treats the sequence as a set, and order has to be injected separately by [[positional-encoding|positional encoding]].

The second is about direction. Nothing in the operation stops position $i$ from reading position $j > i$; row $i$ of the score matrix has an entry for every column. In [[encoder-self-attention|the encoder]] that is exactly what is wanted, since the whole input sentence is available at once.

Auto-regressive generation is a different matter, because there position $i$'s output has to be produced before token $j$ has been generated at all. So the decoder uses [[masked-decoder-self-attention|a masked variant]]. It is built on [[causal-masking|setting the scores for future positions to $-\infty$ before the softmax]], which sends their weights to zero and leaves each position attending only to itself and what came before.

### Why, and what it costs

Section 4 argues the case on [[layer-comparison-desiderata|three axes]], summarised in [[table-1]]. Two of the three are where self-attention is claimed to win, and it is worth taking them one at a time.

Against a [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent layer]], the win is [[minimum-sequential-operations|sequential steps]]. A recurrent layer's state at position $t$ is computed from the state at position $t-1$, which in turn waits on $t-2$, so the positions of one sequence have to be walked in order. Self-attention computes the whole score matrix in one shot, with no row waiting on another. That is a constant number of sequential operations against $O(n)$.

Against [[convolutional-sequence-models|convolutional models]], the win is [[maximum-path-length|path length]]. A kernel of width $k < n$ only reaches $k$ positions at a time, so connecting every pair takes a stack of $O(n/k)$ layers — $O(\log_k n)$ if the convolutions are dilated. Self-attention connects every pair inside a single layer.

The consequence is about signal, not just wiring. The distance a gradient travels between [[long-range-dependencies|distant positions]] stops growing with how far apart those positions are.

The cost sits in the same $n \times n$ score matrix that buys those two wins. Filling it takes $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ work per layer, against a recurrent layer's $O(n \cdot d^2)$. Compare the two and self-attention is the cheaper of them only while $n < d$ — which holds for the word-piece sentences the paper trains on, and fails for long documents.

The paper does propose a remedy: [[restricted-self-attention|let each position attend only to a window of size $r$ around it]]. It is put forward as future work, and no experiment in this paper tests it.

There is a further concession. [[separable-convolutions|Separable convolutions]] reach the same complexity as self-attention plus a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network|feed-forward layer]], so on cost alone the comparison is a draw. Cost is not what carries the argument. Parallelism and path length are.

The direct evidence for the layer itself is thin. [[table-1]] counts operations asymptotically; it is not a measurement of anything that was run.

The visualisations are suggestive rather than systematic. [[fig-3]] shows one query word linking to "more" and "difficult", six and seven tokens away, and [[fig-5]] shows two heads behaving differently on one sentence. Both are single hand-picked examples, and the paper claims only that the patterns "seem related" to sentence structure.

That leaves [[table-2]] as the strong number. It scores the whole architecture, though, not this layer in isolation.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

pages.body:
An [[recurrent-neural-network|RNN]] computes its hidden state as $h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$. That equation is usually read as a formula, but it is also a scheduling constraint. The state at position $t$ takes the state at position $t-1$ as one of its inputs, so the work at position $t$ cannot begin until the work at position $t-1$ has finished.

Unroll it and the constraint gets concrete. To compute $h_5$ you first need $h_4$. To get $h_4$ you first need $h_3$. The chain runs all the way back to the beginning of the sentence, and every link in it has to be walked in order.

So the positions inside a single training example are locked into a queue, and the queue is as long as the sentence. That is the sequential-computation bottleneck.

The paper opens with this because the [[transformer|Transformer]] is the attempt to delete that dependency. Everything else in the architecture follows from deleting it.

### What is actually serialized

Take a batch of $B$ sentences, each of length $n$, with hidden width $d$. The per-step work in a recurrent layer is $W_{hh}h_{t-1} + W_{xh}x_t$, plus whatever gates the [[lstm|LSTM]] or [[gated-recurrent-unit|GRU]] adds on top. Those are $d \times d$ matrices applied to $d$-dimensional vectors, so one step costs $O(d^2)$.

There are $n$ steps in a sentence, and each costs $O(d^2)$. The layer therefore costs $O(n \cdot d^2)$, which is the entry the paper later reports for recurrence under [[complexity-per-layer]].

Total FLOPs are not the issue. A GPU is happy with lots of arithmetic. The issue is the shape of each individual launch.

At step $t$ you multiply a $B \times d$ activation matrix by a $d \times d$ weight matrix. The only dimension along which that operation is wide is $B$. The $n$ positions cannot help fill the machine, because the later ones have not been computed yet.

With $d = 512$ and a modest $B$, a matmul that narrow underfills the device. And you do not pay that cost once — you pay it $n$ times, back to back, which means $n$ separate kernel launches and $n$ separate points of latency.

The paper's second clause matters as much as the first: memory constraints limit batching across examples. Longer sequences hold more activations for backprop, so the memory budget forces $B$ down.

Note when that happens. $B$ has to shrink exactly when $n$ grows. The one axis of parallelism you had left gets narrower precisely as the axis you cannot parallelize at all gets longer. (This is also why the paper batches by length — see [[length-based-batching]].)

[[factorization-tricks]] and [[conditional-computation]] are the prior work the introduction credits, and the paper is careful about what they bought. They delivered real efficiency gains, and in the conditional-computation case better model quality as well.

But look at what they act on. Both of them shrink the cost of a step. Neither reduces the number of steps, and the number of steps is what the queue is made of. That is why the paper says the fundamental constraint remains.

### How strong the evidence is

The direct evidence is [[table-1]]. Its [[minimum-sequential-operations|sequential-operations]] column reads $O(n)$ for a recurrent layer and $O(1)$ for [[self-attention]] — a queue as long as the sentence against a queue of constant length.

Read that column for exactly what it is. It is a count of operations in the abstract, not a wall-clock measurement, and no timing experiment in the paper isolates this variable on its own.

The same table also names the price. A self-attention layer costs $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ per layer against the recurrent layer's $O(n \cdot d^2)$. Divide both by $n \cdot d$ and the comparison reduces to $n$ against $d$: self-attention is the cheaper layer in total compute only when $n < d$.

The paper argues that condition does hold for sentences tokenized into word pieces, where typical lengths sit below the model width. It also notes where it stops holding, which is long documents.

Recurrence is not the only architecture this argument has to clear. [[convolutional-sequence-models|Convolutional models]] had already removed the sequential dependency, so on the parallelism axis they are not the target. What they kept was a [[maximum-path-length]] that grows with the distance between positions, and Section 4 treats that as a separate complaint.

### Two costs of removing recurrence

Recurrence was carrying order information for free: a state that arrives step by step knows what came before it. Delete recurrence and that information disappears, so it has to be put back deliberately by [[positional-encoding]].

The second cost is a limit on what the parallelism buys. It is a *training* property. At inference the model still produces one token at a time, because [[auto-regressive-generation|each generated token is an input to the next]] — the queue returns, just on the output side.
