pages.body:
The Transformer is an [[encoder-decoder-architecture|encoder-decoder]] for [[sequence-transduction|sequence transduction]]. What makes it unusual is what is missing from it: there are no recurrent layers anywhere. Every one of them has been replaced by two components, [[self-attention]] and an MLP applied separately at each position.

The reason is parallelism. An RNN computes its hidden state at position $t$ from the hidden state at position $t-1$, so to get position 5 you first need position 4, and to get position 4 you first need position 3. The positions inside a single training example therefore have to be computed one after another, in order — [[sequential-computation-bottleneck|they cannot be computed at once]]. This model removes that dependency entirely.

### What actually runs

[[fig-1]] is the whole thing in one picture. It is worth walking the data path from the bottom.

Tokens enter through [[token-embeddings|embedding tables]] and come out as vectors of width $d_{model} = 512$, scaled by [[sqrt-dmodel-embedding-multiplier|$\sqrt{d_{model}}$]]. A [[positional-encoding]] is then added to each of those vectors. Without it the model is order-blind: nothing left in the architecture reads order, so there is no way to tell position 3 from position 30, and the same set of vectors would look identical shuffled.

The result is an $n \times 512$ matrix, and that matrix goes up the [[encoder-stack]]. The stack is [[n-layers|six]] identical layers. Each layer is a [[multi-head-attention]] [[sub-layer]] followed by a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]], which widens each position's vector to 2048, applies a ReLU, and projects back down: $512 \to 2048 \to 512$.

Every sub-layer, in both stacks, is wrapped the same way:

$$\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$$

The $x\ +$ is the constraint that propagates. A sub-layer's input is added to its output, so the two must have the same width. The sub-layers are chained, so that width has to be the same everywhere.

That is why every sub-layer and every embedding layer emits 512, and why [[d-model]] is a single number for the whole model rather than one per layer. The shared width is what makes [[residual-connection|the residual add]] type-check.

The [[decoder-stack]] is the same six-layer construction with a third sub-layer inserted into each layer. First comes [[masked-decoder-self-attention|self-attention masked]] so that position $i$ sees only positions $< i$. Then comes [[encoder-decoder-attention]], where the queries come from the decoder and the keys and values come from the encoder's top layer. That middle sub-layer is the only place the two towers touch.

### What the swap buys and costs

Section 4 argues the swap on [[layer-comparison-desiderata|three axes]], tabulated in [[table-1]]. Two of them come out in the Transformer's favour.

Sequential operations — the steps that must run one after another rather than in parallel — fall from $O(n)$ for recurrence to $O(1)$. The path a signal must travel between any two positions falls to a constant, because self-attention connects every position to every other one inside a single layer. Set that against the architectures that had already dropped recurrence: the same path grows linearly with distance in [[convs2s|ConvS2S]], and logarithmically in [[bytenet|ByteNet]].

The costs are stated too. Per-layer compute is $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, because every position attends to every position, so the number of query-key pairs grows with the square of the sequence length. That is cheaper than recurrence only while $n < d$. The condition holds for the word-piece sentences used here, and it stops holding for long inputs. For that case the paper offers [[restricted-self-attention|windowed attention]], where each position attends only to a neighbourhood around it — but offers it as future work, not as a result it measured.

The second cost sits inside the mechanism itself. A single attention output is a weighted sum over all the positions attended to, which makes it [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|an average, and averaging blurs resolution]]: whatever was specific to one position is mixed into the blend.

[[multi-head-attention]] is the paper's stated counter to exactly that. It is a repair for a cost the design created, not an independent idea.

### How strong the evidence is

The headline numbers are in [[table-2]]. The [[base-vs-big-transformer|big]] model reaches 28.4 [[bleu]] on WMT14 English-German, over 2.0 above anything published to date, including [[model-ensembling|ensembles]]. On English-French it reaches 41.8. Both figures come after 3.5 days of training on eight P100s.

One caution on the French number: take it from the table. Section 6.1 prints 41.0 for the same model.

Then there is the shape of the evidence behind those numbers. It covers two language pairs. Each result is a single run, and no variance across runs is measured, so the paper gives no way to judge how much of any gap is noise. The training-cost column is not a measurement either — it is an estimate, formed as GPU-hours times an assumed sustained throughput per GPU.

Generalization rests on one further task. [[table-4]] reports 91.3 F1 on WSJ parsing, beating every listed discriminative parser except [[recurrent-neural-network-grammar|the RNN Grammar]] at 91.7 — and that model builds trees explicitly rather than emitting a flat sequence.

Three tasks in total, all of them text.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

pages.body:
Section 6.2 has one fixed starting point and one rule. The starting point is the [[base-vs-big-transformer|base configuration]]: $N=6$ layers, $d_{model}=512$, $d_{ff}=2048$, $h=8$ heads, $d_k=d_v=64$, $P_{drop}=0.1$, 100K training steps, 65M parameters. The rule is that each experiment changes one of those numbers and leaves everything else exactly where it was.

That second part is what makes the table readable. Any quantity a row does not list as changed still holds its base value. So when an output column moves, the move can be traced back to the single number that was edited.

[[table-3]] is therefore a set of controlled single-variable edits, and that gives it a specific job in the paper. It is the only direct evidence that these particular settings matter — as opposed to the general shape of the model, attention plus a position-wise feed-forward layer with no recurrence, carrying all of the quality on its own.

### What each row reports

Every row is a fresh training run. Same data — [[wmt-2014-en-de]] — same recipe otherwise, scored on newstest2013. That set is the *development* set, not the test set.

Each row carries three columns: per-wordpiece [[perplexity]], [[bleu]], and parameter count. Decoding uses [[beam-search]] with the settings from Section 6.1, with one deliberate difference: no [[checkpoint-averaging]].

Two consequences follow from that scoring setup, and both matter the moment these numbers are compared to anything outside this table.

The first concerns BLEU. The base model scores 25.8 here. The same model scores 27.3 in [[table-2]]. Those two numbers are not in conflict — one is dev-set BLEU and the other is test-set BLEU, measured on different sentences. They are not interchangeable.

The second concerns perplexity. It is measured per wordpiece, under the paper's [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]]-style subword vocabulary. Perplexities reported per word elsewhere are averaged over a different unit, so the two quantities are not comparable.

### Reading the sweeps

Rows (A) vary the number of attention heads $h$, but they hold total computation constant. To keep the total fixed as $h$ grows, [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k$ and $d_v$]] have to shrink in step. At $h=1$, the single head runs at $d_k=512$. At $h=32$, each head runs at $d_k=16$.

So two things move together down that sweep. Head count rises, and per-head width falls.

This limits what the sweep can establish. [[attention-heads-ablation|Quality peaks somewhere in the middle]] of the (A) rows, which invites the reading that there is a best head count. That reading is not clean, because head count and per-head width are confounded in this experiment. Either one could be bending the curve.

Rows (B) pull the two apart. They shrink $d_k$ on its own — 64, then 32, then 16 — with the head count left alone. Quality falls as $d_k$ falls.

The paper reads that as a hint about the scoring function itself: that the dot product may be too simple a [[compatibility-function]] for the job ([[key-size-ablation]]). It is offered as a suggestion drawn from three rows, not as a demonstration.

Rows (C) and (D) [[size-and-dropout-ablation|change model size and regularization]]. The pattern in (C) is that larger models translate better. The pattern in (D) is that dropout is doing real work against over-fitting.

Row (E) is a swap rather than a dial. It replaces the [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|fixed sinusoids]] of [[eq-posenc|the positional-encoding formula]] with [[learned-positional-embedding|learned position vectors]], one trainable vector per position.

The result is 4.92 / 25.7, against the base row's 4.92 / 25.8. Identical perplexity, one tenth of a BLEU apart. No measurable difference.

The paper keeps sinusoids anyway, and the stated reason is extrapolation: fixed sinusoids may let the model handle sequences longer than any it saw during training. Table 3 does not test that. The dev sentences fall inside the training length range, so the extrapolating case never arises in this experiment. On the evidence in this table alone, the choice is a coin flip.

### How strong the evidence is

Each cell is a single training run. Seed variance is not measured and no error bars are reported. Differences of a few tenths of a BLEU therefore carry little weight — nothing here separates an effect that small from ordinary run-to-run noise.

A few gaps are wide enough to clear that bar. Single-head attention sits 0.9 BLEU below the best row of the (A) sweep. The no-dropout row and the $N=2$ row each fall by more than a full point.

One row also has its two metrics pointing in opposite directions. In (D), removing [[label-smoothing]] gives *better* perplexity than the base model and *worse* BLEU.

The paper does not treat that as a puzzle to resolve. It states the trade directly: smoothing hurts perplexity, because it trains the model to be less sure of itself, and it improves BLEU regardless.

Section 5 is where the paper stops describing an architecture and starts describing a run. It gives the exact data, the shape of a batch, the hardware, the optimizer schedule, and the regularizers. Every number in [[table-2]] is the output of these choices.

The section is not an appendix. The paper's headline claim is not only quality but quality per unit of compute, and both halves of that ratio are fixed here — the numerator by the recipe, the denominator by the hardware and the step count.

### The run, concretely

There are two tasks. The first is [[wmt-2014-en-de|4.5M English-German sentence pairs]], tokenized with [[byte-pair-encoding|BPE]] into a vocabulary of about 37000 tokens shared across both languages. The second is [[wmt-2014-en-fr|36M English-French pairs]], with a larger 32000-token [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] vocabulary.

A batch is not a fixed number of sentences. It is roughly 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens. Pairs are [[length-based-batching|grouped by similar length]] before batching, because a 5-token sentence sitting in a batch with a 50-token one gets padded out to 50, and that padding would count against the token budget. At typical sentence lengths, 25000 tokens works out to something on the order of a thousand pairs per step.

The hardware is [[training-hardware-and-schedule|eight P100s in one machine]]. The base model runs at 0.4 seconds per step for 100k steps — 40000 seconds of step time, a little over 11 hours, reported as 12 hours. The [[base-vs-big-transformer|big model]] runs at 1.0 seconds per step for 300k steps, which is 300000 seconds, or 3.5 days. Big is therefore 2.5 times more expensive per step and runs three times as many steps.

[[adam-optimizer|Adam]] is used with [[transformer-adam-settings|$\beta_2 = 0.98$]] rather than the usual 0.999. That is the decay on the running average of squared gradients, so 0.98 averages over a shorter recent window. The paper states the value without justifying it.

The learning rate is not a constant. It is a function of the step number, given by [[eq-lrate|Equation (3)]]:

$$lrate = d_{model}^{-0.5} \cdot \min\left(step^{-0.5},\ step \cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5}\right)$$

Read the $\min$ one branch at a time. Early on, $step \cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5}$ is the smaller of the two, and it grows linearly with the step count. Later, $step^{-0.5}$ is smaller, and it falls as the inverse square root. The crossover is at $step = warmup\_steps$, so the schedule is a [[learning-rate-warmup-schedule|linear ramp followed by inverse-square-root decay]] with its peak at [[warmup-steps-4000|step 4000]].

The peak value is worth computing. With $d_{model}=512$, the front factor $512^{-0.5}$ is about $0.044$; at step 4000 the $\min$ contributes $4000^{-0.5}$, about $0.0158$. Their product is about $7 \times 10^{-4}$.

Two things follow from the form of the equation. First, the rate is scaled by [[d-model|model width]], so a wider model automatically gets a smaller rate and base and big share one schedule with no retuning. Second, the warmup exists because the early steps of a residual stack with [[layer-normalization|layer norm]] are the fragile ones. The paper does not argue that point. It picks the shape and moves on.

Regularization is announced as three types but written up as two. The first is [[residual-dropout|dropout on each sub-layer output, and on the embedding-plus-position sums]], at $P_{drop}=0.1$ for the base model and 0.3 for big EN-DE. The second is [[label-smoothing|label smoothing]] at $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$. The third, [[attention-dropout|attention dropout]], surfaces only later, in [[constituency-parsing|the parsing section]].

Label smoothing is the one cost the paper names outright. It hurts [[perplexity|perplexity]], because the model is trained to put less mass on the correct token and so becomes less sure. It improves [[bleu|BLEU]] anyway, and the paper takes that trade.

### How much of this is actually tested

Less than the recipe's confidence suggests. [[transformer-ablations|Table 3]] does sweep the architecture knobs, and it sweeps [[size-and-dropout-ablation|the dropout rate]] as well. So the claim that dropout is very helpful has support behind it.

The rest does not. Warmup length, $\beta_2$, batch composition, and label smoothing are never varied. They are one point in a space, reported rather than defended.

The compute side is softer still. The cost comparison rests on a [[training-flops-estimate|FLOPs estimate]] — training time multiplied by number of GPUs multiplied by an assumed sustained 9.5 TFLOPS per GPU. That throughput is assumed, not measured.

What makes the recipe reproducible, then, is less the ablations than [[tensor2tensor|the released code]]. Two decode-time steps travel with it: [[checkpoint-averaging|checkpoint averaging]] and [[beam-search|beam search]].

The architecture section makes one structural claim, and it is worth stating plainly before the details arrive. There is only one attention block in the model. The [[transformer|Transformer]] gets three different behaviours out of that single block by changing two things: where the queries, keys and values are read from, and whether one mask is applied.

Everything else inside a layer is a fixed wrapper. The same wrapper goes around every sub-layer in both stacks, and it does not change from one use to the next. So what distinguishes the encoder from the decoder is wiring, not machinery.

### One block, three wirings

Section 3.2.3 lists the three uses of [[multi-head-attention]], and it lists nothing more. Three wirings is the complete inventory.

The first is [[encoder-self-attention]]. Queries, keys and values all come from the same place — the output of the previous encoder layer. Because all three come from one source and nothing is held back, every position sees every position.

The second is [[masked-decoder-self-attention]]. The same three come from a single source again, this time the previous decoder layer, so structurally it is the same wiring. The one difference is the visible range: it stops at the current position.

The third is [[encoder-decoder-attention]], and here the sources split. The queries come from the decoder. The keys and values come from the output of the [[encoder-stack]].

That split has a scheduling consequence. The keys and values do not exist until the encoder has produced its final layer's output, which is why the encoder has to finish before this sub-layer has anything to attend over. It is also why the paper says this sub-layer "mimics" the attention of earlier sequence-to-sequence models: a decoder issuing queries against an already-encoded source is what those models did.

[[fig-1]] draws all three at once. Treat it as a wiring diagram. It fixes what connects to what; it does not fix sizes.

### The mask is the whole difference

Come back to the first two wirings, because the gap between them is smaller than it looks. It is one operation.

[[causal-masking]] sets the scores of forbidden positions to $-\infty$ on the input to the [[softmax]]. This happens inside [[scaled-dot-product-attention|the attention function itself]] — it is the optional Mask box in [[fig-2]], not a separate layer sitting before or after.

The reason it works at all is $e^{-\infty} = 0$. Exponentiating a masked score gives exactly zero, so those positions contribute exactly zero to the softmax's numerator and drop out of the weighted sum entirely. Zero weight, not small weight. Nothing leaks.

The paper's stated reason for wanting this is that leftward information flow has to be prevented to preserve [[auto-regressive-generation|the auto-regressive property]]. And the paper is careful about the credit it assigns: it says the mask does this combined with the one-position offset of the output embeddings. Neither of the two alone is enough.

The cost of the mask is by construction rather than by measurement. A decoder position can only look backwards, so the decoder gives up the encoder's full context.

### The wrapper that forces one width

Now the part that does not vary. Every [[sub-layer]] gets identical treatment — all three attention variants and the feed-forward network alike.

The wrapper is $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$. [[residual-connection|The residual]] adds the sub-layer's input straight onto its output, and that addition is only defined if both sides have the same number of dimensions. That is the constraint every width in the model has to satisfy.

Section 3.1 gives the causal direction explicitly: to facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers and the embedding layers output dimension [[d-model|$d_{model} = 512$]]. Read that in the order the paper writes it. The uniform width is a consequence of the wrapper, not an independent choice.

The normalization half of the wrapper gets less attention in the text. [[layer-normalization]] is used by citation only; the paper never writes the formula. From the cited work, [[layer-normalization-statistics|the mean and variance are taken across the hidden units of one position]] — that position's own activation vector, and nothing else.

That is what lets it apply unchanged to variable-length sequences. Each position is normalized on its own terms, so a short sequence and a long one are handled the same way. [[layer-norm-vs-batch-norm|Unlike batch normalization]], nothing in the computation depends on batch composition.

The second sub-layer in every layer is [[eq-ffn|Equation (2)]], $\max(0, xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2$. $W_1$ expands each position's vector from $512$ up to the inner width [[d-ff|$d_{ff}=2048$]], which is four times $d_{model}$; the $\max(0, \cdot)$ acts elementwise in that wider space; $W_2$ projects back down to $512$, which is what the residual addition needs.

The thing to notice about this [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]] is what it does not touch. It processes one position at a time, with no term anywhere in it that reads another position.

That matters for the argument being built here. Every cross-position interaction in the model happens in an attention sub-layer, and nowhere else.

[[n-layers|$N = 6$]] then stacks the pair. Six identical layers in the encoder, six in the [[decoder-stack|decoder]] — and with that, the [[encoder-decoder-architecture]] is complete.

### What is argued, not measured

Everything above is the paper's own reasoning, and it is mostly definitional. It says what the model is.

What it does not do is test the wiring. [[table-3]] varies head count, $d_k$, model size, dropout and [[positional-encoding]]. It does not vary $N$. It does not remove the residual or the normalization. It does not try an unmasked decoder, and it does not test alternative placements.

So the two load-bearing claims in this cluster are a different kind of thing from the ablation numbers. The claim that masking preserves auto-regression is a correctness argument about what the arithmetic permits, not a result.

The claim that the residual is why the width is shared is the paper's stated motivation. No ablation separates it from the simpler possibility that one width is just convenient.

Read this cluster as a specification, not as evidence.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

pages.body:
Sort the training setup into two piles. In one pile are the choices the paper actually tests: [[table-3]] varies the architecture one knob at a time and reports what happened to translation quality. In the other pile sits the recipe wrapped around that architecture — tokenizer, vocabulary, weight sharing, smoothing, decoding constants.

Almost every item in that second pile arrives the same way. It comes in by citation, it comes in at a fixed number, and it comes in with no experiment attached.

The pattern is not only about borrowing, either. The one recipe piece the authors contribute themselves — the learning-rate schedule — is asserted on the same terms as the imports.

### One borrowed decision constrains the next

The chain starts at tokenization. English-German is encoded with [[byte-pair-encoding]], and the vocabulary is not written down by hand. It is the output of the cited greedy [[bpe-merge-algorithm|merge loop]], which repeatedly fuses the most frequent adjacent symbol pair in the corpus, one merge at a time, until it has performed as many merges as it was asked for.

That loop is where the vocabulary size comes from. Without it, "about 37000 tokens" is a number with no procedure behind it.

Section 5.1 adds one further fact about this vocabulary: it is shared between source and target. That is the [[joint-bpe-shared-vocabulary|joint-BPE]] variant, where the merges are learned over both languages' text at once rather than separately for each. English and German end up drawing tokens from a single inventory.

That shared inventory is what makes the next choice available. [[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing|Section 3.4]] puts one matrix into three roles: encoder input embedding, decoder input embedding, and pre-softmax output projection. It cites [[weight-tying]] and offers no motivation of its own.

The cited work's argument is a contrast with the usual arrangement. Normally a model holds [[input-and-output-embeddings|two separate matrices of the same shape]] — one turning token ids into vectors on the way in, one scoring vectors against tokens on the way out. Tying collapses those two into one. The version that folds in a third role, the encoder's embedding as well, is [[three-way-weight-tying]].

And that third role is only available under a condition. The rows of the matrix are indexed by token id, so the encoder and the decoder have to be reading from the same token inventory in the first place. Joint BPE is what supplies that condition. The tying is therefore downstream of the tokenization choice rather than an independent decision.

English-French breaks the chain. There the vocabulary is 32000 [[word-piece-encoding|word pieces]] from the cited [[wordpiece-model]], a different subword scheme entirely, and the paper never says that this vocabulary is shared across the two languages.

So the precondition that made the three-way tie possible for English-German is not stated to hold for English-French. Whether the tie holds for that model is unstated. That gap is my reading of the text, not something the paper flags.

Sitting on top of the tie is [[sqrt-dmodel-embedding-multiplier]]. In the embedding layers only — not in the output projection that shares the same weights — the values are multiplied by $\sqrt{d_{model}}$. With $d_{model}$ at 512, that factor is $\sqrt{512} \approx 22.6$.

The paper states this in one clause and gives no reason. The multiplier arises only because one matrix is doing two jobs at once. The usual explanation is that the two jobs want the weights at different scales, so one of them has to be rescaled before use; that explanation is a common reading and is not in the paper.

The rest of the imports are single settings, each one a number lifted out of a cited procedure. [[label-smoothing]] at $\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$ is the target mixture from the cited [[label-smoothing-regularization|LSR]] method, which gives the correct token $1 - \epsilon_{ls}$ of the probability mass instead of all of it and spreads the remaining $\epsilon_{ls}$ over the other tokens.

[[length-penalty]] at $\alpha = 0.6$ is the exponent in the cited [[length-normalization-penalty|length normalizer]], the divisor that lets hypotheses of different lengths be compared on a common footing during [[beam-search|beam search]]. It is used with beam size 4 and was picked on the development set. The paper never says what $\alpha$ does.

### The schedule is the paper's own

Equation (3) is the exception to the borrowing — the [[learning-rate-warmup-schedule|schedule]] shown in [[eq-lrate]]:

$$lrate = d_{model}^{-0.5} \cdot \min(step^{-0.5},\ step \cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5})$$

Two things follow from the shape of that expression.

The first is the $\min$. Early on, $step$ is small, so $step \cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5}$ is the smaller of the two terms and the rate climbs linearly with the step count. Later, $step^{-0.5}$ becomes the smaller term and the rate falls. The two terms cross at [[warmup-steps-4000|warmup_steps = 4000]]. That crossing point is where the rate peaks, and after it the rate decays as $step^{-0.5}$.

The second is the prefactor out front. The whole curve is scaled by [[d-model|$d_{model}$]]$^{-0.5}$, so a wider model automatically takes smaller steps without anyone retuning the schedule for it.

What the schedule sets is the global step size. [[adam-optimizer|Adam]] then adapts that global size per parameter on top of it. The two were chosen as a pair: the schedule was picked together with $\beta_2 = 0.98$, which sits below Adam's usual default.

None of those pieces is ablated. No experiment anywhere in the paper varies the warmup length, the decay exponent, or $\beta_2$.

### What is not shown

Table 3 covers heads, $d_k$, model size, dropout, and [[positional-encoding]]. Its rows (D) do include label-smoothing values, so the numbers are on the page. But the prose that discusses those rows talks only about dropout.

The consequence is a small mismatch between evidence and text. The claim that smoothing hurts perplexity while improving accuracy and BLEU is stated more firmly than it is demonstrated.

The borrowed recipe itself is never varied at all. Nothing tests BPE against word pieces, the tying against untied embeddings, the multiplier, $\alpha$, or the schedule.

The cost numbers belong in the same territory for a different reason: they are inference rather than measurement. The [[training-flops-estimate|FLOPs figures]] in [[table-2]] are not counted. Each is training time multiplied by GPU count multiplied by an assumed 9.5 TFLOPS sustained per P100.

Run that through for the largest model. The [[training-hardware-and-schedule|3.5-day, 8-GPU big-model run]] gives roughly $2.3 \times 10^{19}$.

The assumption is carrying the comparison. The efficiency claim holds only if 9.5 TFLOPS sustained is equally fair to the hardware the baselines were trained on.

The case for dropping recurrence rests on an argument from three numbers in a table. It is not an argument from an experiment. The paper does not train a recurrent model and a self-attention model under matched conditions and report which learns long dependencies better; Section 4 sets up a framework and fills it in instead.

The framework is [[layer-comparison-desiderata|three criteria]] for judging any layer that maps a length-$n$ sequence to another length-$n$ sequence. First, [[complexity-per-layer]]: how much arithmetic one layer performs. Second, [[minimum-sequential-operations]]: how much of that arithmetic must run in order rather than all at once. Third, [[maximum-path-length]]: how far a signal has to travel through the network to get from one position to another.

Self-attention wins two of the three on the paper's own accounting. The third — cost — turns out to be conditional, conceded, or tradeable, and the section says so itself.

### The chain

Of the three criteria, path length is the one the argument actually turns on. [[long-range-dependencies]], meaning relationships between symbols far apart in a sequence, are called "a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks."

The mechanism the paper states for why path length matters is distance. A signal travelling between two positions passes through some number of intermediate steps, forwards through the activations and backwards through the gradients. The shorter that path, the easier the dependency is to learn.

That premise is cited to prior work. It is not tested here. Every conclusion downstream of it rests on it holding.

[[table-1]] is the framework filled in with complexity classes, and without it Section 4 is a list of assertions. Its path-length column gives $O(1)$ for [[self-attention]], $O(n)$ for a [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent]] layer, and $O(\log_k n)$ for [[dilated-convolutions|dilated convolutions]].

The recurrent entry is worth reading concretely. To produce the hidden state at position 5, the layer needs the hidden state at position 4. To get that one, it needs position 3, and so on back to the beginning of the sequence. Two positions $n$ apart are therefore separated by $n$ of these steps, one chained after another.

The sequential-operations column shows the same structure from the other side: $O(1)$ for self-attention against $O(n)$ for recurrence. Those $n$ steps cannot be computed simultaneously, because each one waits on the result of the one before it. That is the [[sequential-computation-bottleneck]], restated as a complexity class.

So the two columns each say one thing. Self-attention connects any two positions in a single step, and it computes every position at the same time. Recurrence does neither.

[[convolutional-sequence-models]] sit between the two, and the paper treats them as a partial fix that stopped short.

A convolutional layer does compute all positions in parallel, so the sequential-operations problem is already solved there. But a kernel of width $k < n$ only spans $k$ positions, so a single layer does not connect every pair. Covering the whole sequence takes $O(n/k)$ stacked layers, or $O(\log_k n)$ layers if the convolutions are dilated.

That is where the two cited models land. [[bytenet]] pays logarithmically in the distance between the two positions being related; [[convs2s]] pays linearly. Neither reaches a constant. That is why the background section lists them together rather than as rival answers.

### Where the criteria disagree

The three criteria do not rank the layer types in the same order, and the paper does not hide it.

Start with per-layer cost. Self-attention compares every position against every other position, at width $d$, giving $O(n^2 \cdot d)$. A recurrent layer instead does one $d \times d$ matrix multiply at each of the $n$ positions, giving $O(n \cdot d^2)$. Setting $n^2 d$ against $n d^2$ cancels one factor of $n \cdot d$ from each side and leaves $n$ against $d$. Whenever $n > d$, recurrence is the cheaper layer.

The paper's answer is that in the regime it cares about, $n < d$ instead. Sentence-length sequences in subword vocabularies come out shorter than the model is wide. It points at [[byte-pair-encoding]] and [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] as the tokenizations that produce those sequences — 37000 and 32000 tokens respectively in its own two experiments, against $d_{model} = 512$.

That is a condition, not a result. It is also a condition set from outside the architecture, by the tokenizer. The BPE paper's own [[vocabulary-vs-sequence-length-tradeoff]] states the coupling directly: finer subword splits shrink the vocabulary and lengthen every sentence. Split finer and $n$ climbs back toward $d$.

Two further moves push in the same direction.

The first concerns convolutions again. The paper grants that [[separable-convolutions]] bring the cost down to $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$. Take $k$ all the way to $n$, so that the kernel spans the entire sequence, and that expression equals the cost of a self-attention layer plus a point-wise feed-forward layer. That is the exact combination the Transformer stacks in each of its layers.

The second runs the trade in the opposite direction. [[restricted-self-attention]] has each position attend only to a neighborhood of size $r$ around it, which makes the layer cheaper on very long sequences. The bill arrives in the path-length column, where the maximum rises from $O(1)$ to $O(n/r)$.

Read those two moves together and the shape of the case shows. Cost is not what carries it. Parallelism and path length are.

### What the argument does not establish

Several gaps separate what Table 1 shows from what the case needs.

Table 1 shows that the path is short. It does not show that models with short paths learn distant dependencies better. That link is the premise cited to prior work, arriving here as a conclusion.

The sequential-operations column counts operations abstractly. It measures parallelizability, not wall-clock time on a GPU, and no timing is reported to stand behind it.

The r-neighborhood row is analysis rather than experiment. Restricted attention is proposed and its complexities are entered in the table, but the paper never trains it.

[[fig-3]] is the only picture in the paper of a long dependency actually being tracked. It is one query word, in one sentence, in one [[encoder-self-attention|encoder self-attention]] layer. It shows that long-distance attention happens. It does not show how often, or how reliably.

And the constant-length path is not free. The paper admits the [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|averaging cost]]: a single attention operation blends many positions into one weighted average, which can blur position-specific information. [[multi-head-attention]] is introduced as the counteraction to that.

Finally, nothing here isolates the variable. No ablation separates path length from everything else the architecture changed at once.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

pages.body:
The paper's attention layer is not a new mechanism. It is two edits to a mechanism that already existed.

Section 3.2 makes three moves, in order. It picks plain dot-product scoring, and it picks it for speed. It then adds a single divisor, to repair the failure that this scoring choice is already known to have once the dimension gets large. Finally it runs the repaired function eight times in parallel, to repair a second failure that the paper blames on averaging.

Only the last of those three moves arrives with a measurement attached. That asymmetry runs through the whole section.

### A speed choice with a known failure mode

Two scoring functions were on the table: [[dot-product-attention]] and [[additive-attention]]. The paper calls them similar in theoretical complexity.

It picks the dot product anyway, and the reason is implementation rather than theory. Scoring one query against every key by dot product is a matrix multiplication, and matrix multiplication has heavily optimized code behind it. The paper's claim is that this makes dot-product attention much faster and more space-efficient in practice.

Then, in the same paragraph, it states the price of that choice. Additive attention outperforms unscaled dot-product attention at larger $d_k$. The faster option is the worse option once the key dimension grows.

[[sqrt-dk-scaling|The divisor]] is the repair, and the paper argues for it in a footnote. The argument is a variance calculation.

Assume the components of a query $q$ and a key $k$ are independent, with mean 0 and variance 1. The dot product $q \cdot k$ is a sum of $d_k$ products of such components. Each of those products has mean 0 and variance 1, so the sum has mean 0 and variance $d_k$. Its typical magnitude therefore grows like $\sqrt{d_k}$. The divisor is exactly that quantity, so the scores stop growing with dimension.

The stated reason this matters is about [[softmax]]. Large dot products push the softmax into a region where its gradients are extremely small, and a function with extremely small gradients is hard to train through.

The paper does not claim to have demonstrated that. Its own wording is "we suspect", and it runs no ablation on the factor.

Those two decisions together — the dot product for speed, the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ for the softmax — give [[scaled-dot-product-attention]]. [[eq-attention|Equation (1)]] writes the whole function in one line:

$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Read left to right, that is four steps: score every query against every key, shrink the scores by the divisor, normalize them into weights, and use the weights to combine the values.

The left panel of [[fig-2]] redraws the same line as a data flow diagram. It shows one thing the equation hides, which is where the mask sits. It sits after the scale and before the softmax.

### Head count and head width are the same decision

[[eq-multihead|The MultiHead equation]] looks like a second mechanism. It is not. It is a wrapper around the first one.

[[multi-head-attention]] does four things in sequence. It projects $Q$, $K$ and $V$ down to a smaller width, once per head, with that head's own learned matrices. It calls Equation (1) inside each head. It concatenates the per-head outputs. It maps that concatenation back to full width through $W^O$. The scoring rule inside never changes.

Running eight copies of an attention layer would ordinarily cost about eight times as much as running one. What keeps it affordable is the width rule: [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h$]].

Work that out for the base model. [[d-model|$d_{model}$ is 512]], and [[num-heads-h|$h$ is 8]], so each head gets $512/8 = 64$ dimensions for its queries, keys and values. The 64 in the paper is not a tuned choice. It falls out of the other two numbers.

Because each [[attention-head]] is that narrow, the paper says the total computational cost stays close to that of a single attention over full-width vectors. Eight heads of width 64 do roughly the arithmetic of one head of width 512.

The right panel of [[fig-2]] draws that side of it, showing the $h$ heads running beside one another. The `Concat` in the equation does not make the parallelism visible.

That accounts for the cost of running more than one head. It does not account for the reason.

The reason is [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|the averaging argument]], and the argument is asserted rather than derived. Section 2 supplies the first half. Attention buys a constant path length between any two positions, but it does so "at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions" — one weighted average over many positions blurs what any individual position contributed.

Section 3.2.2 adds a single sentence: "With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this." Multiple heads are offered as the counter. No analysis follows either sentence.

### What the numbers cover, and what they don't

[[table-3]] row (A) is the measured part of all this. It varies [[attention-heads-ablation|the head count with total computation held constant]], so as $h$ rises each head is made narrower to compensate. The comparison is between shapes, not between budgets.

Two results come out of that row. Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting. Quality also drops off again when there are too many heads.

That establishes two things. $h$ matters, and its effect is non-monotone — there is a best head count somewhere in the middle, not a direction to keep pushing in.

It does not establish that the heads occupy distinct representation subspaces. A single narrow head being worse than eight is consistent with several explanations, and the subspace story is only one of them.

That story rests on inspection instead of measurement. [[attention-interpretability|Attention visualizations]] such as [[fig-4]] and [[fig-5]] show heads in the same layer, run on the same sentence, behaving differently from each other. The sentences are hand-picked, and no metric is attached to any of them. They are illustration, not evidence of the kind row (A) provides.

The divisor, meanwhile, has no experiment at all. Nothing in [[table-3]] varies the scaling factor.

The closest thing in the table is row (B), where [[key-size-ablation|shrinking $d_k$ hurts quality]]. The paper reads that as evidence that a dot product may be too simple a compatibility function.

That reading is a note filed against its own opening argument. The dot product was chosen for speed, and here the paper records a reason to doubt it is the right function. It leaves the note unresolved.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

pages.body:
Take recurrence out of a sequence model and the first thing you notice is what you gained. In a recurrent layer the hidden state at position 5 cannot be computed until position 4's state exists, and position 4 is waiting on position 3. That chain is the [[sequential-computation-bottleneck|sequential computation bottleneck]], and dropping recurrence dissolves it.

The second thing takes longer to notice. That same chain was the only thing telling the model which token came first. Order was riding along inside the computation, and when the computation goes, order goes with it.

These links are the paper's accounting of that debt. [[self-attention]] cannot see order on its own. [[positional-encoding]] has to put it back. And the particular scheme the paper ships is picked on a hypothesis rather than on a measurement.

### Order was a side effect, not a feature

A [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent layer]] never represents position explicitly. Nothing in the hidden state is a slot that says "this is token seven." The layer gets order for free from the order in which it consumes tokens — position is implicit in the shape of the computation.

Self-attention has no such shape. It computes a weighted sum over all positions at once, and a sum does not care in what order its terms arrive. Permute the inputs and the outputs permute with them, values unchanged. The layer has no handle on who came first.

Section 3.5 says it flatly: since the model contains no recurrence and no convolution, information about relative or absolute position "must" be injected some other way.

So the positional encoding is not an extra feature bolted onto the design. It is a repair for something the design removed. It is the one place in the architecture where that trade shows up as a cost rather than a saving.

### What gets added

[[eq-posenc|Equation (4)]] fixes the repair as a bank of sinusoids. The vector added at each position is as wide as the model itself, $d_{model} = 512$ dimensions, and each of those dimensions holds one sine or cosine evaluated at the position — even dimensions sine, odd dimensions cosine:

$$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\!\left(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}}\right), \qquad PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}}\right)$$

What separates one dimension from the next is frequency, and the dimension index enters only through the exponent $2i/d_{model}$. At the first pair of dimensions $i = 0$, so the divisor is $10000^{0} = 1$ and the wavelength is $2\pi$: that dimension completes a full cycle every $2\pi$ positions. At the far end of the bank the exponent approaches 1, the divisor approaches 10000, and the wavelength approaches $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ — across a whole sentence that dimension barely moves. The wavelengths in between run in a geometric progression from one end to the other.

Nothing in that bank is learned. There are no parameters here, only a formula, which is what lets [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|the scheme]] produce a vector for a position it has never seen. Position 900 is exactly as computable as position 9.

Note the operation as well as the values. The vector is *added* to the token embedding, not concatenated, so content and position share the same 512 dimensions rather than each getting a block of its own. Nothing in the architecture keeps the two apart. The model has to separate them itself.

The paper's stated reason for choosing this family is [[relative-position-linearity|the offset property]]. Fix any shift $k$. Then $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$, and it is the same linear map at every $pos$ — within each frequency, a rotation by a fixed angle. That is the property the authors "hypothesized would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions."

Hypothesized is their word, and the two halves of that sentence do not stand on the same footing. The linearity is a fact about the formula, a per-frequency rotation, checkable on paper with no model involved. That the trained model actually exploits it is not shown anywhere: no probe, no ablation isolating it.

### The comparison that came out flat

[[learned-positional-embedding|A trainable vector per position]] is the obvious alternative — throw out the formula and let the position vectors be parameters like any others. The paper tried it. [[table-3|Table 3]] row (E) reports nearly identical results.

That matters because the same ablation table does separate other choices. The [[attention-heads-ablation|head-count sweep]] in that table moves BLEU by 0.9 between single-head attention and the best setting. Against a table with that much resolution, the sinusoid-versus-learned swap moves nothing worth reporting.

Quality did not decide the question.

The tiebreak was extrapolation. Sinusoids "may allow" the model to handle sequences longer than any seen in training: a position past the training range still has a formula, where a learned table has no row for it. The paper does not test this. Both translation benchmarks are sentence-level, so the long inputs that would separate the two schemes never come up, and the plan for genuinely long inputs is deferred to future work ([[restricted-self-attention]], and the conclusion's note about local attention for images and audio).

So the chain has two halves of unequal strength. That positional information must be injected is argued directly from the architecture, and it is not in doubt. That it should be injected *this way* rests on one flat comparison and one untested property of the formula.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

pages.body:
Everything the paper claims about working outside translation rests on this one experiment. There is no second generalization task in the paper. The weight of the abstract's phrase "generalizes well to other tasks" sits entirely on English constituency parsing.

Read as a chain, the experiment establishes less than that phrase suggests. Two things get in the way. The task had to be converted into the paper's own problem format before the architecture could be run on it at all. And the headline result arrives with a named exception.

### The task has to be reshaped first

[[constituency-parsing|English constituency parsing]] produces a nested tree. A sentence goes in, and what comes out is a hierarchy of phrases inside phrases — not a string.

The [[transformer|Transformer]] decoder emits one token at a time and nothing else. It has no operation for opening a subtree, no stack, no way to attach a child to a parent. So parsing cannot be run on this architecture as it stands. It can only count as [[sequence-transduction]] once the tree has been flattened into a token sequence.

That flattening is done by [[parse-tree-linearization]]. The traversal walks the tree depth-first, emitting a bracket-and-label token on entering a node and a closing token on leaving it. The tree comes out as a string of brackets. The scheme is taken unchanged from the cited setup.

The paper does not restate that scheme and does not defend it. That is worth noticing. The step that makes the generalization test possible is not part of the contribution being tested.

The model itself never handles a tree, at any point in training or decoding. It handles a string that happens to decode into one. Nothing in the architecture enforces that the brackets balance — that property has to come out of the learned distribution or not at all.

The paper does say what makes this target harder than a translation target. The output is under strong structural constraints. It is also much longer than the input.

### Two regimes, and what separates them

Two models are trained here, and the thing that changes between them is training data. Both follow [[wsj-parsing-protocol|the standard WSJ protocol]]: tune on Section 22, report F1 on Section 23. That shared protocol is what makes [[table-4|the table]] comparable to prior parsers at all, since every number in it was produced on the same held-out section.

The first regime is the small-data one. It trains on the [[penn-treebank-wsj|WSJ treebank]] alone, about 40K hand-parsed sentences. The model is 4 layers deep, with [[d-model|$d_{model}$]] = 1024 and a 16K vocabulary. It reaches 91.3 F1.

The second regime keeps the task and enlarges the data. The [[semi-supervised-parsing|semi-supervised setting]] adds roughly 17M machine-parsed sentences from the [[semi-supervised-parsing-corpora|high-confidence and BerkeleyParser corpora]]. It reaches 92.7.

The higher of those two numbers is not the interesting one. The small-data row is the one carrying the argument.

RNN sequence-to-sequence models had not reached state of the art with 40K sentences. On that data the classical [[berkeley-parser|BerkeleyParser]] was the reference point — the score a WSJ-only parser had to clear. The Transformer passes it.

That comparison is the paper's own, and it is the specific thing translation results could not have shown. The translation experiments all ran on millions of sentence pairs. Nothing in them speaks to what happens at 40K examples.

### What the numbers do not settle

Start with the tuning claim, which the paper qualifies itself. The phrase it uses is "only a small number of experiments," and that hedge is doing real work — but it is not a claim of no tuning.

Four things were selected on Section 22: [[residual-dropout|residual dropout]], [[attention-dropout|attention dropout]], the learning rate, and [[beam-search|beam size]]. Everything else was inherited unchanged from the [[base-vs-big-transformer|base translation model]]. "Little task-specific tuning" is a fair summary of that. "None" is not.

Next, what is missing around each number. Each regime is a single reported run. There are no seeds and no variance reported, so no gap between scores here can be checked against run-to-run noise.

There is also no ablation of which architectural property helped. The parsing section tests the whole model or nothing.

The two regimes differ in more than their training data. The vocabulary also changes, from 16K in the WSJ-only run to 32K in the semi-supervised one. So the +1.4 F1 gap is not a clean measurement of what 17M extra sentences buy. Two variables moved at once, and the paper does not separate them.

Finally, the ceiling, which the paper makes explicit. [[recurrent-neural-network-grammar|RNNG]] builds trees with tree-structured operations rather than emitting brackets as text, and it scores higher than the Transformer here. The paper states this plainly in the body. The abstract does not.

So the honest reading of this cluster is narrower than "generalizes." A generic sequence model, barely tuned, is competitive with specialized parsers on one English task. And a model with structure built in still wins.

The claim these links add up to has two halves. One [[transformer|Transformer]], trained once, beats the prior systems on translation. The same model also costs less to train than they did.

There is a third thing the links say, quieter than the first two. The specific settings inside that model — how many heads, how wide the keys, how much dropout — were picked by measurement. None of them is derived from anything.

The evidence behind those claims is not uniformly strong. It thins as you follow the chain down. [[table-2]] is a benchmark result on a standard test set. [[table-3]] is a development-set sweep on a single language pair. [[fig-4]] and [[fig-5]] are two hand-picked pictures.

### Quality and cost as two axes

[[machine-translation|Translation]] is the paper's instance of [[sequence-transduction]], the general problem of turning one sequence of symbols into another. The headline number comes from [[wmt-2014-en-de]]: about 4.5M sentence pairs, encoded with a byte-pair vocabulary of roughly 37000 tokens shared between the two languages.

On that task the big model reports 28.4 [[bleu|BLEU]]. That is more than 2.0 BLEU above the best previously reported result, and the comparison set includes ensembles, not just single models.

The French result is reported twice and not identically. On [[wmt-2014-en-fr]], the larger set at 36M pairs, Section 6.1 says 41.0 while the abstract and the table say 41.8. Read the French number off the table.

Next to every score, Table 2 puts a [[training-flops-estimate]]. That column is what converts a quality claim into a quality-per-cost claim: 41.0 at less than a quarter of the previous state of the art's training cost.

It is worth being exact about where that column comes from. The figure is training time multiplied by the number of GPUs used, multiplied by an *assumed* sustained throughput for each GPU type — 2.8, 3.7, 6.0, and 9.5 TFLOPS for the K80, K40, M40, and P100 respectively. No operations are counted anywhere in that product.

So the cost axis is an estimate and the BLEU axis is a measurement. The cost axis is the softer of the two.

Two of the paper's comparisons ride on that softer axis. One is a single model set against [[model-ensembling|ensembles]], where the cost gap is most of the point. The other is the Transformer against [[convs2s]], which is how the paper argues that dropping convolutions — not just recurrence — cost nothing.

[[base-vs-big-transformer|Base and big]] appear as separate rows rather than as one headline configuration. That split supports a second, weaker, cheaper claim: even the base model surpasses all previously published models and ensembles.

### Where the base model's constants come from

Table 3 changes one thing at a time and reports the effect. Rows (A) sweep the number of attention heads while holding total computation fixed.

Holding computation fixed is only possible because each head's width is $d_{model}/h$ rather than the full model width — see [[dk-dv-dimensions]]. In the base model $d_{model}$ is 512 and $h$ is 8, so each head works in $512/8 = 64$ dimensions. Double the head count to 16 and each head drops to 32. The widths across all heads still sum to 512, so the arithmetic per layer barely moves.

The sweep's result has two ends. Single-head attention lands 0.9 BLEU below the best setting. Quality also falls off with too many heads.

That one sweep is the entire basis for [[num-heads-h|h = 8]], and for the [[attention-heads-ablation|middle-is-best reading]] of head count generally. It is one development set, on one language pair.

Rows (B) give [[key-size-ablation]]: shrinking the key dimension $d_k$ lowers translation quality. From that number the paper moves to a broader statement — that determining [[compatibility-function|compatibility]] is not easy, and that something more sophisticated than [[dot-product-attention|the dot product]] may be beneficial.

That move is an interpretation, not something the table tests. The rows vary one dimension of the existing scoring function; no alternative scoring function is run. The interpretation is a caveat the authors place on their own choice.

Rows (C) and (D) get a single sentence between them: [[size-and-dropout-ablation|bigger is better, dropout helps]]. Row (D) is what justifies $P_{drop} = 0.1$ for [[residual-dropout]].

But (D) varies a single rate, and that one rate is applied in several places in the recipe at once. So it does not separate residual dropout from dropout applied anywhere else.

Row (E) swaps the sinusoids out for [[learned-positional-embedding|learned position vectors]] and gets nearly identical results. That removes any quality argument for the sinusoids.

They are kept anyway, on an untested hope: that a fixed periodic encoding may let the model extrapolate to sequences longer than the ones it was trained on. The table says nothing about that.

### Where the metrics disagree

[[label-smoothing]] of 0.1 makes [[perplexity]] worse and BLEU better. The paper keeps it.

The two measures are not actually contradicting each other. Perplexity grades how much probability mass the model puts on the reference token, and smoothing deliberately holds some of that mass back, so perplexity has to get worse. BLEU grades the tokens that decoding actually emits, and those got better.

Still, this is the one place in the paper where the two measures point in opposite directions. It is also a reason to report translation quality in BLEU rather than in likelihood.

One caution about how firmly this is established. Section 6.2's prose about Table 3 discusses dropout and never mentions smoothing. The trade-off is asserted more firmly than it is demonstrated.

### What the figures do not show

A single attention operation collapses many positions into one weighted average, and an average of many things carries less about any one of them. [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost|That blurring of position-specific information]] is the paper's stated reason for running several heads instead of one.

[[fig-4]] is the illustration of that reason. Heads 5 and 6, in the same encoder layer, put the word "its" on two different words. [[attention-interpretability]] — the idea that individual heads take on distinct roles — rests on [[fig-5]].

Both are selected examples with no quantitative analysis behind them. The paper hedges its readings of them as "apparently" and "seems related".

Nothing measured connects head diversity to the 0.9 BLEU that rows (A) report. The picture and the number sit next to each other without a link between them.

The model has one computational primitive. Everything else in the architecture is scaffolding around it — stacking it, wrapping it, feeding it. This page covers two things: what that primitive does, and why the paper's version of it carries two extra pieces the generic version does not. The first extra piece is a division by $\sqrt{d_k}$. The second is eight copies of the whole function running side by side.

### The generic function, then the specific one

[[attention-mechanism|Attention]], as Section 3.2 defines it, is deliberately unspecific. It takes a query vector and a set of key-value pairs. Out comes a weighted sum of the values. That is the entire definition.

[[queries-keys-values|The three roles]] are all the structure there is. A query asks for something. Keys advertise what each position has on offer. Values carry the content that actually gets mixed into the output.

The weight placed on each value comes from a [[compatibility-function]], which scores the query against that value's key; those scores become the weights after a softmax. Note what the definition does not say. It never says what the scoring function is. That empty slot is the one the paper fills.

[[scaled-dot-product-attention]] fills it with a dot product, softmaxed, with a single rescaling in between. [[eq-attention|Equation (1)]] is the whole thing:

$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Read it left to right. $QK^{\top}$ scores every query against every key in one matrix multiply. The division by $\sqrt{d_k}$ shrinks those scores. The softmax turns each row of scores into weights, and multiplying by $V$ takes the weighted sum.

The choice of a dot product is a choice about speed, not about expressiveness. The paper puts [[additive-attention]] — a scorer built as a net with one hidden layer — as comparable to the dot product in theoretical complexity. The difference shows up in practice instead. A dot product drops straight into optimized matrix-multiply code, so it is faster and uses less memory. [[dot-product-attention|Plain dot-product attention]] is this same algorithm minus the one scaling factor.

That factor is there because of a reported failure. Prior work found that additive attention outperforms unscaled dot-product attention, and that the gap widens as $d_k$ grows. So the plain dot product is fine at small key dimension and degrades at large key dimension.

The paper's explanation for that is a suspicion, and it is stated as one. The suspicion is that large dot products push the softmax into regions where its gradients are very small. The supporting argument is a footnote rather than an experiment: if the components of the query and key are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, then their dot product has mean 0 and variance $d_k$. Variance $d_k$ means the typical magnitude of a score grows like $\sqrt{d_k}$. [[sqrt-dk-scaling|Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$]] cancels exactly that growth.

Put the two halves next to each other. The fix is applied in every attention call in the model, on the strength of a variance calculation and a suspicion about where the softmax ends up. The evidence for the mechanism is thinner than the confidence with which the fix is adopted.

This is what makes [[dk-dv-dimensions|$d_k$ and $d_v$]] load-bearing quantities rather than incidental ones. $d_k$ sets the scale of the raw scores, and it is the quantity $\sqrt{d_k}$ is compensating for.

There is a later data point on the same dimension. [[table-3]] reports that [[key-size-ablation|shrinking $d_k$ costs quality]]. The authors read that as a hint that a dot product may be too simple a compatibility function after all.

### Why eight of them

[[multi-head-attention]] sits directly on top of Equation (1). Each head is one call to that same function, unchanged. The only additions are linear projections before the call and a concatenation after it. [[eq-multihead]] states it.

The motive comes from a cost the paper admits back in the Background. Attention relates any two positions in a constant number of steps, however far apart they are. But the way it does that is by averaging over positions, and an average blurs the detail that belongs to any single position — [[attention-averaging-resolution-cost]].

Running $h$ attentions on separate subspaces is the counter to that. [[attention-projection-matrices|Learned projections $W^Q_i, W^K_i, W^V_i$]] map each [[attention-head|head]]'s inputs down into that head's own lower-dimensional space.

Work the sizes out. [[d-model|$d_{model}$ is 512]], and there are [[num-heads-h|$h = 8$ heads]], so each head gets $d_k = d_v = d_{model}/h = 512/8 = 64$ dimensions. A fourth matrix, $W^O$, mixes the concatenated head outputs back up to the full width of 512.

Now the cost. Each head is narrower than the full model by a factor of $h$, so each head's attention is correspondingly cheaper to compute. Eight of them together cost close to what one full-width head costs. The extra resolution is bought at nearly no extra computation. [[fig-2]] draws both halves — Equation (1) on the left, the parallel copies on the right.

That is the argument. Support for the part of it claiming that heads occupy "different representation subspaces" is mostly pictures. [[fig-3]], [[fig-4]] and [[fig-5]] show heads whose attention patterns are visibly different from one another. The paper's own wording about [[attention-interpretability|what heads learn]] is guarded: the behavior "seems related" to sentence structure.

The measured claim is smaller than the interpretive one. [[attention-heads-ablation|Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse]] than the best head count. And the curve turns over at the other end — too many heads also hurts.

### What comes next

[[fig-1]] and [[transformer|the architecture]] gave you a layout with attention-shaped holes in it. You now have the thing that fills them, in both its single-head and its eight-head form.

The next question is not what attention computes. That function is fixed now, and it does not change again anywhere in the model. The question is where $Q$, $K$ and $V$ come from on each call.

That sourcing is the only thing distinguishing [[encoder-self-attention]], [[masked-decoder-self-attention]] and [[encoder-decoder-attention]]. Three uses, one unchanged function.

pages.body:
Attention moves information between positions. Every output vector it produces is a blend of vectors that came from somewhere else in the sequence.

That leaves two things undone. Nothing has yet transformed a position's own vector on its own terms. And nothing has told the model which slot in the sentence a token actually sits in.

Three pieces close both gaps, and together they finish the layer.

### The other half of every layer

In [[fig-1|the model diagram]], a layer is not one block but two. An attention [[sub-layer|sub-layer]] comes first, and a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]] comes second. [[eq-ffn|Equation 2]] is the entire second half:

$$\mathrm{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$$

Read it left to right on a single position's vector. That vector has width $d_{model}=512$. The first matrix $W_1$ widens it to [[d-ff|$d_{ff}=2048$]], four times as wide. [[relu|ReLU]] zeroes the negatives at that width. The second matrix $W_2$ projects the result back down to 512, so the vector leaves the sub-layer the same size it entered.

Two details about the weights. Within one layer, the same $W_1$, $W_2$, $b_1$, $b_2$ are applied at every position — position 1 and position 40 go through identical arithmetic. Across layers, each layer has its own set.

The paper offers a second reading of the same operation: two convolutions with kernel size 1. A kernel of width 1 touches exactly one position and never its neighbours.

Note what this block is not. It never looks sideways.

That matters because of what the attention sub-layer produced. Attention's output at a position is a weighted average of value vectors — weights aside, it is linear in those values. All the cross-position mixing has already happened, and it happened linearly. So the feed-forward block is where per-position nonlinear transformation lives, and it is the only place in the layer where it lives.

The paper does not argue for this division of labour. It states the shape of the block and moves on.

The block is also not small. Each layer holds two $512 \times 2048$ matrices, which is $2 \times 512 \times 2048 \approx 2.1$ million weights. The same layer's [[multi-head-attention|attention projections]] are four $512 \times 512$ matrices, about 1.05 million weights. The feed-forward half carries roughly double the parameters of the attention half.

### One matrix doing three jobs

[[embedding-softmax-weight-sharing]] is what it sounds like. The encoder's [[token-embeddings|input embedding]] table, the decoder's input embedding table, and the projection that turns the decoder's final vectors into vocabulary logits are not three matrices. They are one matrix used three times.

The paper does this by citation. It points at [[weight-tying]] and does not restate why tying helps.

There is also no ablation for it here — no row that turns sharing off and reports the cost. So treat it as a parameter-count and convention choice the paper inherited, rather than as something this paper tested.

The one wrinkle is the [[sqrt-dmodel-embedding-multiplier]]. In the two embedding roles, the shared weights are multiplied by $\sqrt{d_{model}}$. With $d_{model} = 512$, that factor is $\sqrt{512} \approx 22.6$, so the embeddings come out about twenty-two times larger than the raw shared weights would give.

The paper states this in a single clause and gives no reason for it. The usual reading is that a matrix whose scale suits producing softmax logits produces embeddings that are too small — too small in absolute terms, and too small relative to what gets added to them next.

### Telling the model where it is

Start from a property of the mechanism. [[self-attention]] is permutation-equivariant: shuffle the input tokens, and the outputs come back in the shuffled order, individually unchanged. Nothing inside the attention computation distinguishes "the third token" from "the tenth"; there is no recurrence walking left to right and no convolution window to fix an ordering.

So order has to be supplied from outside. That is the entire reason [[positional-encoding]] exists.

It is supplied once, at the bottom of each stack, added to the input embeddings. It is not re-injected at every layer.

[[eq-posenc|The encoding used]] is [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding|a bank of fixed sinusoids]] — fixed in the sense that nothing about them is learned. Each dimension of the vector is a sine or a cosine evaluated at the position index. The dimensions differ in wavelength, and those wavelengths form a geometric progression from $2\pi$ at one end to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ at the other.

The encoding has width $d_{model}$, which is what allows it to be summed with the embedding instead of concatenated to it. That choice is why the embedding's scale mattered in the previous section: the two vectors land on top of each other, so their relative sizes are a real design variable.

Two reasons are given for sinusoids over the alternative, and the paper hedges both.

The stated hypothesis is [[relative-position-linearity]]: for any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$. A head that wants to attend "three positions back" would therefore need to learn a linear map rather than something position-specific, which the paper suggests should make attending by relative position easy to learn.

The second reason is extrapolation. Because the sinusoids are a formula rather than a lookup table, they are defined at positions longer than anything seen in training, and the paper says this "may allow" the model to handle such sequences. That is a conjecture, and the paper does not test it.

Against [[learned-positional-embedding|learned position vectors]], the measured results are near-identical ([[table-3]], row E). The empirical case for sinusoids is therefore not a quality case. The choice rests on the untested extrapolation argument.

### What this sets up

The layer is now fully specified. Attention, feed-forward, residual connections around each, and a single order signal added at the bottom of the stack.

One question is still open. Nothing so far explains why the attention half is there at all, rather than recurrence or convolution.

That is what [[layer-comparison-desiderata|three criteria]] and [[table-1]] take up next.

pages.body:
Black out every formula in the paper and something is still there: the wiring diagram. This theme is about that diagram — the shape of [[transformer|the Transformer]], which you can hold in your head before any attention math arrives. [[fig-1]] is the whole thing in one picture.

### It keeps the old frame

The paper does not propose a new way to organize a translation model. It keeps the [[encoder-decoder-architecture]] that competitive sequence models already used.

That frame has two halves. An encoder maps the input symbols $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ to continuous representations $z = (z_1,\dots,z_n)$. A decoder then reads $z$ and emits output symbols one at a time.

Generation stays [[auto-regressive-generation|auto-regressive]]. The decoder produces one symbol, that symbol is fed back in as part of the decoder's input, and the next symbol is produced conditioned on it. Nothing about that loop changes here.

That continuity is the point. [[theme-why-recurrence-had-to-go|The previous theme]] argued only that the *inside* of a layer should stop being recurrent. The outer contract — encoder, decoder, one symbol at a time — is unchanged.

So what follows is a swap of layer internals. It is not a redesign of the task.

### Two stacks of one layer, repeated

Each half is a stack of $N=6$ identical layers ([[n-layers]]). Identical here means identical in shape, not in weights. Each of the six layers has its own parameters, but every layer is built from the same components in the same arrangement. Describing one layer therefore describes all six.

The [[encoder-stack|encoder layer]] holds two [[sub-layer|sub-layers]]. The first is multi-head self-attention. The second is a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]], which runs the same small network on position 1's vector, then on position 2's vector, and so on down the sequence — separately, and with identical weights at every position ([[eq-ffn]]).

The [[decoder-stack|decoder layer]] has those same two sub-layers, plus a third inserted between them. So the decoder layer runs self-attention, then the new sub-layer, then the feed-forward network. That third one attends over the encoder's output.

This is where the two towers meet. [[encoder-decoder-attention]] draws its queries from the decoder, but takes its keys and values from the top of the encoder stack. It is the only channel through which any information about the input reaches the decoder at all.

The decoder also modifies its self-attention. Positions may not attend to later positions ([[masked-decoder-self-attention]]). A decoder position can look at itself and at everything to its left, and nothing else. Combine that restriction with output embeddings offset by one position, and the prediction at position $i$ can depend only on outputs before $i$.

That is the auto-regressive property from the frame above. Note where it now comes from. A recurrent decoder got it for free, because at step $i$ it simply had not computed steps $i+1$ onward yet. Here every position is computed at once, so the same guarantee has to be written into the layer as a structural restriction rather than falling out of processing order.

### One wrapper around everything

Every sub-layer, in both stacks, is wrapped the same way:

$$\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$$

Two operations are stacked in that line. The [[residual-connection]] adds each sub-layer's input back onto its output, which leaves the sub-layer responsible only for learning a change on top of the identity. If $\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$ came out as zero, the wrapper would pass $x$ straight through. Then [[layer-normalization]] rescales each position's vector, using a mean and variance computed across that one vector's own features ([[layer-normalization-statistics]]) — not across the batch.

The paper treats this wrapper as part of what a sub-layer *is*, rather than as a tuning choice applied afterwards. There is no unwrapped sub-layer anywhere in the model.

The wrapper is also the reason the model has a single width throughout. Look at the addition $x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$: it is elementwise, so the input vector and the output vector must have the same number of dimensions. That constraint chains through the network, because one sub-layer's output is the next one's input. And it reaches back to the embeddings, since the very first thing a stack adds a residual to is an embedding vector.

The paper says explicitly that all sub-layers and the embedding layers output vectors of dimension $d_{model} = 512$ ([[d-model]]), *to facilitate these residual connections*. The constant width is a consequence of the residual, then, not an independent design decision.

### What the shape forces next

Two things fall out of the picture so far.

The first is about order. Nothing in this architecture carries information about position — there is no recurrence and no convolution, and every remaining piece treats the sequence as a set. Permute the input positions and the same layer would produce the same output vectors, just permuted along with them.

Order is real information about a sentence, and none of it survives that permutation. Position therefore has to be injected, once, from outside the layers. The paper adds it to the embeddings at the bottom of each stack ([[eq-posenc]]).

The second is about what is left unexplained. Every layer's actual substance now sits inside sub-layers you have not seen the math for yet.

That is the handoff. The shape has fixed three attention slots: self-attention in the encoder, masked self-attention in the decoder, and the decoder's attention over the encoder output. You can now read [[theme-how-attention-is-computed|how attention is computed]] knowing exactly which three slots it has to fill, and where each slot's queries, keys, and values come from.

As for whether the shape works, that argument comes later and rests on two pieces of evidence. [[table-2]] is the headline result on translation. [[table-4]] shows the same stack transferring to [[constituency-parsing]] with little tuning.
