The architecture is settled by now. This theme answers a different question: what do you actually have to do to get the reported numbers, and which of those choices are doing work rather than just being reported?

### Data, tokens, and what counts as a batch

The [[transformer-training-recipe]] starts with two datasets. [[wmt-2014-en-de|WMT 2014 English-German]], about 4.5M sentence pairs, is the main task. [[wmt-2014-en-fr|English-French]], at 36M pairs, is the larger-data check on the same recipe.

Neither dataset is tokenized into words. English-German uses [[byte-pair-encoding]], with a single shared source-target vocabulary of about 37000 tokens covering both languages. That vocabulary is built by the greedy [[bpe-merge-algorithm|merge loop]]: count every adjacent symbol pair in the corpus, merge the most frequent one into a single new symbol, then count again and repeat. Rare words end up split into pieces that the model has already seen. English-French uses a 32000-token [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece vocabulary]] instead, a different scheme in the same subword family.

Subwords are not a side detail here. A subword vocabulary keeps the sequence length $n$ small relative to the model width $d_{model}$. That relationship is exactly the condition the paper's [[layer-comparison-desiderata|cost comparison]] turns on: a self-attention layer costs on the order of $n^2\cdot d$ per layer and a recurrent one costs $n\cdot d^2$, so self-attention is the cheaper of the two only while $n$ stays below $d$.

So the tokenizer choice and the architecture argument lean on each other. A tokenization that made sentences much longer would eat into the cost advantage that motivates the layer in the first place.

Batching has a similar shape. Attention cost is set by the longest sequence in a batch, because every shorter sequence gets padded out to that length and the padded positions consume compute like real ones. Padding is therefore expensive, not free.

[[length-based-batching]] answers that in two moves. Sentence pairs of similar length are grouped into the same batch, so there is little to pad. And the batch is then sized in tokens — roughly 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens — rather than in sentences. Every step sees about the same amount of real signal, whatever the sentences happen to be.

### The learning rate is a schedule, not a number

[[training-hardware-and-schedule]] is a single machine with 8 P100 GPUs. The base model runs 100,000 steps, which takes 12 hours. The big model runs 300,000 steps, three times as many, and takes 3.5 days — see [[base-vs-big-transformer]] for what else changes between the two.

Those totals are small. At 100,000 steps there is no long stretch of training in which a bad start quietly washes out, so what happens in the first few thousand steps is a real part of the result. That is where [[learning-rate-warmup-schedule|the warmup schedule]] comes in ([[eq-lrate]]):

$$lrate = d_{model}^{-0.5}\cdot\min(step^{-0.5},\ step\cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5})$$

Read the $\min$ term by term. Early on, $step\cdot warmup\_steps^{-1.5}$ is the smaller of the two, and it is linear in $step$, so the rate climbs on a straight line. The two arguments cross exactly when $step$ reaches $warmup\_steps$, which the paper sets to [[warmup-steps-4000|4000]]. After that crossing, $step^{-0.5}$ is smaller and takes over, so the rate decays as the inverse square root of the step number.

The peak, in other words, is not a tuned constant. It falls out of where the two branches meet.

The $d_{model}^{-0.5}$ factor sits outside the $\min$ and scales the whole curve. Because it shrinks as the model gets wider, a wider model receives proportionally smaller steps at every point in the schedule. That is why the same formula carries over from base to big with no retuning of the peak ([[d-model]]).

[[transformer-adam-settings|Adam is run with]] $\beta_2 = 0.98$ rather than the usual 0.999. $\beta_2$ sets how fast the running average of squared gradients forgets, and 0.98 forgets faster than 0.999 does. The practical effect is a shorter memory of past gradient magnitudes, so the per-parameter step sizes track a changing gradient scale more quickly.

The paper states this setting, and it states the warmup schedule, and that is all it does with them. It offers no ablation for either. So the account just given of why they help is inference, not a paper claim.

### Regularization, and the last thing before decoding

Three regularizers ride along with the training run. The first is [[residual-dropout]], applied in two places: to the output of each sub-layer before that output is added back into the residual stream, and to the sums of the token embeddings and the positional encodings. The rate is 0.1 for base, and higher for the big English-German model.

This is the one recipe item with real evidence behind it. [[table-3]] varies the dropout rate directly, and the paper reports dropout as very helpful against overfitting.

The second is [[label-smoothing]] with $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$. The one-hot target is replaced by the mixture from [[label-smoothing-regularization]]: the correct token keeps $1-\epsilon_{ls}$ of the probability mass, and the remaining $\epsilon_{ls}$ is spread across the other tokens. The model is therefore trained never to be fully certain about anything.

The paper is candid about the trade this makes. Smoothing hurts [[perplexity]], which is the direct consequence of training the model to be less certain than the data. It improves accuracy and [[bleu]] anyway. That trade-off is a single reported sentence, not an isolated experiment.

The third comes after training rather than during it. [[checkpoint-averaging]] takes the last 5 checkpoints for a base model, or the last 20 for a big one, written 10 minutes apart, and averages them elementwise into the weights that actually get evaluated. So the reported model is never a model that existed at any single training step. Also unablated.

Everything here ran in [[tensor2tensor]], the codebase the authors released.

With the recipe laid out, you can read [[table-2]] for what it is. It plots quality against training cost, and the cost side of that plot is the schedule described above. The question to carry into it is which of these knobs are specific to this model — the warmup, the $\beta_2$, the $d_{model}$ scaling — and which are ordinary practice carried over from elsewhere.

Everything so far has been design: what the model is, and how it was trained.

This part answers a different question, and really it is two questions. How do you get a sentence out of a trained model? And what evidence is there that any of the design choices earned their place?

### Getting an output at all

A trained decoder does not hand you a translation. At each step it hands you a distribution over the next token, and nothing more. Something has to turn that run of distributions into one string of text.

The paper's answer is [[beam-search]] at beam size 4. Instead of committing to the single highest-scoring token at each step and never looking back, the decoder keeps the 4 best partial sequences alive, extends every one of them, and re-ranks. A token that looks second-best right now can still win, if what follows it scores well.

Two adjustments come with beam search. Both of them are patches on ways the search misbehaves when left alone.

The first is about length. A beam's score is the sum of the log-probabilities of the tokens in it, and every log-probability is negative, so every additional token drags the total down. A short output therefore scores higher than a long one by default, whatever their relative quality. The [[length-penalty|length penalty]] with $\alpha = 0.6$ divides that bias back out.

The second is about stopping. Nothing in the search forces a beam to ever emit an end-of-sequence token, so an unterminated beam could keep extending forever. There is an [[inference-length-limit|explicit cap]] instead: the output may run to the input length plus 50 tokens, and no further.

Both of those numbers, the beam size and the $\alpha$, were picked on the development set. Read them as tuned constants, not as quantities derived from the model.

One last detail about the weights being decoded. They are not the weights left standing at the final training step. They are an elementwise average of the last several saved checkpoints ([[checkpoint-averaging]]) — a choice that belongs to the [[transformer-training-recipe|training recipe]] rather than to decoding.

### Two axes, and one metric that disagrees

Quality is reported as [[bleu|BLEU]]: n-gram overlap against reference translations, with a penalty for outputs that come out too short.

[[perplexity]] is reported as well, and the paper is clear about something awkward in the pairing. The two metrics can move in opposite directions on the same change.

[[label-smoothing]] is the case in point. It deliberately stops the model from putting all of its probability mass on the correct token, so by construction it makes the model less confident, and that *hurts* perplexity. It improves BLEU anyway.

That disagreement is why the headline claims are stated in BLEU. A better-calibrated next-token distribution is not automatically a better translator.

The second axis is cost. The paper wants to claim it wins on quality and on cost at the same time, and that second half is harder to state than it sounds: the prior systems it is being compared against were trained on different hardware, so wall-clock hours do not compare across rows.

The [[training-flops-estimate]] is the workaround. It is training time, multiplied by the number of GPUs, multiplied by an *assumed* sustained single-precision throughput for each GPU — somewhere between 2.8 and 9.5 TFLOPS depending on which card that row used. Two of those three factors are reported facts. The third is a guess at how much of a card's peak the training run actually held. So this is a coarse estimate rather than a measurement, and the paper presents it as one.

[[table-2]] is where the two axes are put side by side. On English-to-German the big model reports 28.4 BLEU, more than 2.0 above every prior row in the table, ensembles included. On English-to-French it reports 41.0, at under a quarter of the previous best model's estimated training cost.

The base model is worth reading separately. It already clears the prior rows on English-to-German, at roughly $3.3 \times 10^{18}$ FLOPs.

### Which knobs mattered

[[transformer-ablations|Table 3]] takes the base model and changes one design choice at a time, measuring the effect on the English-to-German development set. Four of its rows are worth pulling out.

[[attention-heads-ablation|Head count]] has a middle rather than a direction. One head is 0.9 BLEU below the best setting. Pushing the head count too high drops quality off as well.

The detail that makes that row mean something is how the sweep was run: total computation was held fixed across it. Adding heads therefore made each head narrower rather than making the layer bigger. Nothing was gained in capacity between the settings, so whatever [[multi-head-attention|multi-head attention]] is contributing, it is not simply more parameters to work with.

[[key-size-ablation|Shrinking $d_k$ hurts]] quality. The paper reads that as a hint that the dot product may be too simple a compatibility function, and that a more elaborate scoring function could do better. This is a caveat aimed at the paper's own core design choice, and it is stated as a suggestion rather than as a result.

[[size-and-dropout-ablation|Bigger models are better, and dropout helps a lot]]. Neither half of that is surprising.

The last row is the one that undercuts an earlier argument. Learned positional embeddings ([[learned-positional-embedding]]) score almost exactly the same as [[eq-posenc|the sinusoids]]. The case made earlier for sinusoids was that they might extrapolate to sequence lengths never seen in training. These numbers do not support that case; they only show the two options are interchangeable at the lengths tested.

### Does it carry to another task

[[constituency-parsing|Constituency parsing]] is the generalization test. It differs from translation in two ways that matter: the output is longer than the input, and the output is not free-form, because a parse has to obey strong structural constraints.

A tree is not a sequence, so it does not fit a sequence model as it stands. It has to be flattened into a token string first, which is [[parse-tree-linearization|linearization]], borrowed from prior work rather than invented here.

With almost no retuning for the new task, a 4-layer model trained on the roughly 40K sentences of the [[penn-treebank-wsj|WSJ treebank]] reaches 91.3 F1 ([[table-4]]). That is past [[berkeley-parser|BerkeleyParser]], and past every discriminative parser listed there but one: [[recurrent-neural-network-grammar|RNNG]], at 91.7. Training in the [[semi-supervised-parsing|semi-supervised setting]] takes it to 92.7.

That gives you a question to carry back through the rest of the paper. For any claim made earlier: which table is it standing on, and how thin is the margin?

You have the attention function. The question now is where the model actually puts it, and why the same function needs three different wirings to build a translator.

Section 3.2.3 gives the answer. [[multi-head-attention]] appears three times in the model, and the only thing that changes from one use to the next is where the queries come from and where the keys and values come from. Nothing about [[eq-attention|the formula]] changes between them — same dot products, same scaling, same softmax, same weighted sum of values.

[[fig-1]] shows all three uses in one picture: two towers, no recurrence, no convolution.

### Encoder: every position, every other position

[[self-attention]] is the case where queries, keys, and values are all read from the same place. In [[encoder-self-attention]], that place is the output of the previous layer of the [[encoder-stack]].

So each position plays both roles at once. It sends out a query asking for what it needs, and it also offers a key and a value that every other position's query can pull on. What comes back is a weighted mix of all positions, itself included, and the layer computes that mix for every position in one step.

The paper's reason for wanting this is in Section 4, not Section 3. Section 4 compares layer types on three axes: how much computation one layer costs, how many operations have to run strictly one after another, and how far a signal has to travel to get from one position to another.

That third axis is the one to hold onto. [[table-1]] reports that a self-attention layer connects any two positions with a [[maximum-path-length|path of length 1]], and does it in a constant number of sequential steps. Position 1 and position 40 are one weighted average apart, no matter how far apart they sit.

A [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent layer]] needs $O(n)$ of both. The reason is the way it is built: the state at position 5 is a function of the state at position 4, which is a function of the state at position 3, and so on back to the start. Information from position 1 has to be carried through every intermediate state to reach position 40, and those states cannot be computed at the same time.

Convolutions sit in between. [[convolutional-sequence-models|ConvS2S and ByteNet]] relate two distant positions in a number of operations that grows with the distance between them, because a kernel only spans a fixed window. A single convolutional layer therefore does not connect everything; you need a stack of them, and the stack has to be deep enough to cover the gap.

Short paths are argued to make [[long-range-dependencies]] easier to learn. That is the case for self-attention, and it is an argument about learnability, not a measurement of it.

The cost side is where self-attention gives something back. Its per-layer complexity is $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, since every one of the $n$ positions scores against every other, and each of those $n^2$ scores costs work proportional to the representation width $d$. A recurrent layer's is $O(n \cdot d^2)$: one step per position, and each step a $d \times d$ matrix multiply.

Which is cheaper depends on the sentence. Divide both by $n \cdot d$ and the comparison collapses to $n$ against $d$. Self-attention wins only when $n < d$ — when the sequence is shorter than the model is wide. That holds for word-piece sentences. It does not hold for long documents.

The paper has an escape hatch for that case: [[restricted-self-attention]], where a position attends only to a neighborhood around it. It is proposed and left to future work. No experiment in the paper measures it.

Two consequences follow immediately from the encoder wiring.

The first is about order. A position mixes all the others using weights that depend on content, not on where the content sits, so nothing in the layer tells it what order the tokens are in. Shuffle the input and the same weighted averages come back out. That is why [[positional-encoding]] exists at all, added once at the bottom of each tower.

The second is about resolution. One weighted average over the whole sentence blurs things — a single distribution has to serve every purpose the position has at once. So the paper runs the attention in parallel heads instead. [[fig-3]] and [[fig-5]] show different heads within one encoder layer picking out different words in the same sentence.

The paper calls this a qualitative illustration. It says the patterns only "seem" to track sentence structure, and offers [[attention-interpretability]] as a side benefit, with no measurement behind it.

### Decoder: the same layer, minus the future

The decoder wants self-attention for the same reason the encoder does. It cannot have the full version.

The reason is what the decoder is for. It generates one token at a time, and conditions each token on what it has already emitted. During training the whole target sentence is present, so an unmasked decoder position would be able to see positions that come after it — which is to say, read the answer it is being asked to predict.

[[masked-decoder-self-attention]] fixes this with [[causal-masking]]. Before the [[softmax]], the scores for forbidden positions are set to $-\infty$. Exponentiating $-\infty$ gives zero, so those positions come out of the softmax with exactly zero weight and contribute nothing to the mix.

That single line is what preserves [[auto-regressive-generation]]. Combined with output embeddings offset by one position, it gives the property the paper needs: predictions at position $i$ depend only on outputs before $i$.

### Between the stacks

The third use is the one that makes this a transduction model rather than two separate encoders sitting next to each other.

In [[encoder-decoder-attention]], the two sides of the function come from different stacks. Queries come from the previous [[decoder-stack|decoder]] layer. Keys and values come from the encoder's output. Every decoder position can therefore look at the entire input sentence.

This one is not masked. The input is fully available from the start — there is no future to hide.

The paper says plainly that this mimics the encoder-decoder attention of earlier seq2seq models. What is new is that it is the same function as the other two uses. The [[queries-keys-values|query/key/value]] split is what lets one function serve all three roles.

You should now be able to look at any attention [[sub-layer]] in [[fig-1]] and say two things about it: where its Q, K, and V come from, and whether it is masked.

Next comes what has to be bolted on because attention alone is not enough — position information, and the per-position feed-forward network.

pages.body:
The paper's opening move is a complaint, not a proposal. Before it describes a single thing it builds, it has to establish that something is wrong with the field as it stands.

The claim is that the dominant approach to [[sequence-transduction]] has a defect. Not a weakness that a better initialization or a longer training run would close, but one that no amount of tuning removes.

### The task and the incumbent

Sequence transduction is the task of mapping one sequence of symbols to another. The paper's benchmark for it is [[machine-translation|translation]]: a German sentence goes in, an English sentence comes out.

The incumbent architecture was the [[recurrent-neural-network|RNN]], usually in one of its gated forms — the [[lstm]] or the [[gated-recurrent-unit|GRU]]. The paper's own words for these models are "firmly established as state of the art."

That phrasing matters. This is not a setup for knocking down weak baselines. The complaint is a different shape: these models are not too weak, they are shaped wrong for the hardware they run on.

### The defect is structural

A recurrent model factors its computation along the positions of the sequence. The hidden state $h_t$ is a function of exactly two things: the previous hidden state $h_{t-1}$, and the input at position $t$. That one line of dependency is the whole story, and two consequences fall out of it.

The first consequence is about parallelism. To compute the hidden state at position 5, you need the state at position 4. To get position 4, you need position 3. The chain runs back to the start of the sentence, and no position can begin until its predecessor has finished. This is the [[sequential-computation-bottleneck]]: within a single training example, positions cannot be computed in parallel.

There is an obvious reply. If positions inside one sentence must run in sequence, fill the hardware with many sentences at once and parallelize across examples instead.

The paper adds the detail that makes the bottleneck bite. At long sequence lengths, memory limits how much you can batch across examples. So the parallelism lost inside an example cannot be bought back between examples either.

The second consequence is about distance. For a signal to travel from one position to another far away, it has to pass through every intermediate hidden state on the way — $O(n)$ steps for a sequence of length $n$. The paper claims that shorter paths make [[long-range-dependencies]] easier to learn.

Now read the way the paper treats two prior lines of work aimed at this same problem: [[factorization-tricks]] for LSTMs, and [[conditional-computation]]. It does not dismiss either one. It credits both with real gains in computational efficiency.

Then it says the constraint "remains."

That word is the hinge of the whole theme. Both methods make each sequential step cheaper. Neither one reduces how many sequential steps there are. If the quantity that hurts is the count of steps, savings inside a step cannot touch it — the fix has to change the architecture, not the arithmetic.

### The escape routes already tried

[[convolutional-sequence-models]] — [[extended-neural-gpu]], [[bytenet]], and [[convs2s]] — went after the parallelism half of the problem, and on that half they succeeded. A convolution does not wait on the previous position's output, so all positions can be computed at once.

The other half survives. A kernel of width $k$ looks at only $k$ neighbouring positions at a time, and whenever the sentence is longer than the kernel, $k < n$, one layer does not connect every pair of positions.

Reaching the distant pairs means stacking layers until their receptive fields meet. That takes $O(n/k)$ stacked layers with ordinary convolutions, or $O(\log_k n)$ layers with [[dilated-convolutions]], whose kernel taps are spaced apart so each layer covers a wider span.

So distance still costs operations. For ConvS2S the cost grows linearly with the distance between two positions; for ByteNet it grows logarithmically. The path-length problem has not been removed. It has come back in a milder form.

The paper also notes a cost on the other side of the trade. A convolutional layer is more expensive per layer than a recurrent one, by a factor of $k$ — unless the model uses [[separable-convolutions]], which split the operation into cheaper parts.

[[end-to-end-memory-networks]] went after the other half instead. They are built on a recurrent attention mechanism rather than on recurrence aligned to the positions of the sequence.

The paper cites them as evidence that attention can carry a model on its own. It is careful about how far that evidence reaches: the results are on simple-language question answering and language modeling, not on transduction.

A pattern runs through all of it. Each prior attempt buys one property by giving up the other. None of them gets parallel positions and short paths at the same time.

### What the theme sets up

[[table-1]] is where this argument stops being prose and becomes numbers. It scores layer types against the three criteria laid out in [[layer-comparison-desiderata]].

Put [[self-attention]] against those criteria. Every position is connected directly to every other position, so the [[maximum-path-length]] between any two of them is 1. All of those connections happen at the same time, so the number of sequential operations is constant — it does not grow with $n$ at all.

A recurrent layer is $O(n)$ on both of those counts. A convolutional layer is better on the first and needs the stack of layers described above for the second.

The per-layer cost is where the trade shows. A self-attention layer costs $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, because each of the $n$ positions attends to all $n$ positions using $d$-dimensional vectors. A recurrent layer costs $O(n \cdot d^2)$: $n$ steps in sequence, each one a matrix multiplication of size $d \times d$.

Compare the two and self-attention wins only when $n < d$ — when the sentence is shorter than the representation is wide. That is a conditional win, and the paper states the condition rather than hiding it.

One thing to hold onto before leaving Table 1. Everything in it is asymptotic analysis, not measurement. The empirical case arrives later, in the translation results and in the parsing numbers of [[table-4]].

Two costs come with the trade, and both of them drive design decisions later in the paper.

The first is resolution. Attention returns a weighted average over positions, and averaging blends things together, which can blur information specific to any one position ([[attention-averaging-resolution-cost]]). That blurring is the paper's stated reason for [[multi-head-attention]].

The second is order. Recurrence carried order in its own machinery: it processed the first token, then the second, so sequence position was implicit in the wiring. Drop recurrence and that information goes with it.

Look at [[fig-1]] with this in mind. Nothing anywhere in that picture knows which token came first. Order has to be supplied deliberately, injected at the bottom of each stack.

From here you can read any Transformer design choice as an answer to a single question: what did recurrence do for us that we now have to do another way?

pages.body:
By now the architecture is fully specified. Every part has been named and wired together. What the specification cannot supply on its own is a reason to build it that way — why anyone should swap a recurrent layer for a self-attention one at all.

Section 4 is the paper's answer. It is an argument from three numbers rather than from experiment: the case rests on properties you can read off an architecture before you train it.

### The three criteria

The comparison is set up narrowly, and deliberately so. The paper considers three layer types that all do the same job: map a variable-length sequence $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ to another sequence of the same length, with each $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

That is the kind of layer that sits inside any [[sequence-transduction]] encoder. Because the three do the same job, they are genuine substitutes for one another, and the comparison is between drop-in replacements rather than between whole models. On that footing, the paper judges them by [[layer-comparison-desiderata|three criteria]].

The first is [[complexity-per-layer|total computation per layer]] — the arithmetic bill, counted as a function of the sequence length $n$ and the representation width $d$.

The second is [[minimum-sequential-operations]]: how much of that arithmetic has to happen in a fixed order rather than all at once. In a recurrent layer, the hidden state at position 5 cannot be computed until position 4's hidden state exists, and position 4 is waiting on position 3. The work is not merely large — it is ordered, and no amount of hardware collapses the order.

That ordering is the [[sequential-computation-bottleneck]] the paper opened with, and criterion two is its direct restatement. The paper treats the count of ordered steps as its proxy for how parallelizable a layer is.

The third is [[maximum-path-length]]: the longest route a signal must travel between any two positions, going forward through the network or backward through the gradient.

The third criterion is where the argument actually lands, and it exists because of [[long-range-dependencies]]. The paper calls learning them a key challenge in sequence transduction. It then asserts that shorter forward and backward paths make them easier to learn — an assertion supported by a citation rather than by its own evidence.

The gap between those two things is worth stating plainly. Path length is a structural property: you can count it off an architecture diagram without running anything. Ease of learning is not that kind of property at all.

The chain from the first to the second is the load-bearing assumption of the whole section. The paper does not test it directly.

### What the numbers say

[[table-1]] turns the three criteria into big-O expressions, one row per layer type.

Take criteria two and three first, because they are the clean ones. [[self-attention]] connects every position to every other in a single operation, so it needs $O(1)$ sequential steps and any two positions are separated by a path of length 1. A [[recurrent-neural-network|recurrent]] layer needs $O(n)$ on both counts: $n$ ordered steps, and a signal travelling between the ends of the sequence passes through every state in between.

That is the whole case for the swap. Two of the three criteria point the same way, and by a factor that grows with sequence length rather than by a constant.

Criterion one is the one that could have gone against them. Self-attention costs $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ per layer, against a recurrent layer's $O(n \cdot d^2)$.

Those two are worth comparing directly. Both carry a factor of $n \cdot d$; strip it out and what remains is $n$ on the self-attention side against $d$ on the recurrent side. So self-attention is the cheaper layer exactly when $n < d$ — when the sequence is shorter than the representation is wide — and the more expensive one when the sequence is longer.

The paper does not hide this. It argues the condition usually holds for sentence-level translation, where the input is segmented with subword vocabularies like [[word-piece-encoding|word-piece]] and [[byte-pair-encoding|byte-pair]] units, which keep token counts near word counts. With $d_{model} = 512$ (see [[d-model]]), the threshold is a specific number: the layer is cheaper on any sentence shorter than 512 tokens.

That reframes what has been established. It is a claim about how long sentences tend to be, not a general result about the two layer types.

[[convolutional-sequence-models|Convolutional layers]] are handled the same way, and the sticking point is again path length. A kernel of width $k < n$ only mixes positions inside its own window, so a single layer does not connect all pairs. Reaching every pair takes a stack: $O(n/k)$ layers with ordinary convolutions, or $O(\log_k n)$ with [[dilated-convolutions]] as in [[bytenet]].

Logarithmic growth beats [[convs2s]]'s linear growth. Neither is constant, which is what self-attention offers.

Cost is a separate matter from path length, and here the paper gives ground. [[separable-convolutions]] cut the arithmetic bill substantially. The paper concedes that at $k = n$ their complexity matches that of a self-attention layer plus a [[position-wise-feed-forward-network]] — which is exactly the combination a Transformer layer is built from.

### The escape hatch, and the qualitative evidence

The $n^2$ term is the weak point, and it does not stay small. On very long sequences $n$ exceeds $d$ and the cost argument reverses.

The paper sketches a way out. In [[restricted-self-attention]], each position attends only to a window of size $r$ around it rather than to the whole sequence. That buys back the cost, but it spends the thing the section was arguing for: maximum path length rises from 1 to $O(n/r)$.

It is a proposal, not a result. Nothing is trained with it; it is flagged as future work in both Section 4 and the conclusion.

The section closes on a side benefit, [[attention-interpretability]]. [[fig-3]] shows the illustration: several heads link "making" to "more difficult" seven tokens away, in one hop — the path of length 1, visible on an actual sentence.

That is an example, not a measurement. No score is attached to it.

You can now say precisely what the paper claims self-attention buys, and where it is asserting rather than showing. Next comes the recipe that produced the numbers backing any of it.
